posts.title: Hinduism and Business Ethics: Dharma at the Counter
posts.description: Business ethics in Hinduism, in plain terms: artha within dharma, the Tirukkural on fair measures, the blessed account book, and what it asks of a modern job.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: Hinduism never asked traders to be poor; it asked them to be straight. Artha, wealth, sits among the four aims of life, but always inside dharma, like water inside a riverbank.

## What does Hinduism business ethics look like at the counter? — artha held within dharma, the Tirukkural's chapter on impartiality with its image of the true balance and its praise of traders who guard others' goods as their own
## Shubh and labh: auspicious profit — the two words painted by the doors of North Indian shops, the new account book blessed on Diwali, and why profit is honoured only when it is clean
## Does it still apply in an open-plan office? — a sales target, a quarterly report, a vendor who offers a favour; how an old frame of artha within dharma helps with decisions far from any shop
Close: When the account book is blessed at Diwali, in a shop or only in your mind, use it as a yearly look back: not only how much came in, but how it was earned.
takeaways: Hindu business ethics place artha, wealth, inside dharma: earning is honoured, but only by fair means.
The Tirukkural praises the level balance and the trader who protects others' interests as his own.
Customs like writing shubh labh and blessing account books on Diwali tie profit to what is auspicious and clean.

faq.q: What does dharma in business mean?
faq.a: Dharma in business means earning within the bounds of right conduct: honest weights and measures, fair prices, keeping promises and not harming others for gain. Hindu thought treats artha, wealth, as a legitimate aim of life, but places it under dharma. Profit made by deception is not considered true prosperity, however large it looks.

faq.q: What is the meaning of shubh labh?
faq.a: Shubh means auspicious and labh means profit or gain. The two words are often written on either side of a shop's doorway or on account books in North and West India, sometimes linked with Ganesha, whose sons in some traditions bear these names. Together they express the wish that profit should come in an auspicious, righteous way.

faq.q: What does Hinduism say about the ethics of wealth?
faq.a: Hinduism honours wealth as one of the four aims of life, alongside dharma, desire and liberation. The Tirukkural and many Puranic stories praise earning honestly, spending on family and guests, and giving generously. Hoarding, deceit and arrogance about money are criticised. Lakshmi is said to stay where there is order, cleanliness and generosity.

posts.title: Kubera's Story: The God of Wealth Who Was a Treasurer
posts.description: The Kubera story: the god of wealth who lost Lanka to his brother Ravana, became treasurer of the gods, and was humbled by a hungry Ganesha at his own feast.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: Kubera is called the god of wealth, but in most stories he does not own the treasure; he guards it. The Kubera story is really about the difference.

## The Kubera story in the epics — Vaishravana, lord of the yakshas, ruler of golden Lanka, whose half-brother Ravana takes his city and his flying chariot, the Pushpaka; told in the Ramayana and retold in the Puranas
## Treasurer of the gods and guardian of the north — Kubera settled in Alaka, keeper of the nine treasures, one of the guardians of the directions; why homes and shops honour the north for him

## What happened when Kubera fed Ganesha? — the folk story of the lavish feast meant to show off his riches, the child who ate everything and was still hungry, and a handful of rice from Shiva that finally satisfied him
Close: Try thinking of one thing you own as something you are keeping for a while rather than something you have; notice how that changes how you use it.
takeaways: Kubera is the treasurer of the gods and guardian of the north, the keeper of wealth rather than its owner.
In the Ramayana tradition he loses Lanka and the Pushpaka chariot to his half-brother Ravana and settles in Alaka.
A popular folk story has Ganesha eat Kubera's entire feast, a gentle lesson that wealth cannot satisfy hunger that pride creates.

faq.q: What is the Kubera and Ganesha story?
faq.a: In a popular folk telling, Kubera invited Shiva to a grand feast to display his wealth. Shiva sent the child Ganesha instead, who ate every dish and then began eating the palace itself, still hungry. Kubera begged Shiva for help, and a small handful of rice given with love finally satisfied Ganesha. It teaches humility about riches.

faq.q: Who is Kubera in Hinduism?
faq.a: Kubera, also called Vaishravana, is lord of the yakshas and the treasurer of the gods. He is one of the dikpalas, guardians of the directions, keeping the north. Epics describe him as the half-brother of Ravana, who took his city of Lanka. He is usually shown as a stout figure holding a pot or purse of treasure.

faq.q: Why are Kubera and Lakshmi worshipped together?
faq.a: Lakshmi is the goddess of prosperity itself, and Kubera is the guardian and distributor of wealth. Many families invoke both at Diwali, especially on Dhanteras, and some traders include Kubera when blessing new account books. The pairing reflects a traditional idea: fortune comes through grace, and it must also be kept and managed with care.

posts.title: Why Lakshmi Is Called Restless: Wealth That Moves
posts.description: Why Lakshmi is restless: the Vishnu Purana tells how she left Indra, why she is called Chanchala, and what her sister Alakshmi says about keeping prosperity.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: Lakshmi is called Chanchala, the restless one, because she does not stay put; the stories say she leaves when she is taken for granted, and comes back when she is welcomed.

## Why Lakshmi is restless: the day she left Indra — the Vishnu Purana's account of Durvasa's garland thrown down by Indra's elephant, the sage's curse, and fortune slipping out of heaven until the ocean was churned
## Who is Alakshmi? — the elder sister in folk tradition who follows quarrels, clutter and neglect; why houses are swept and lamps lit before Lakshmi is invited
## Why should wealth move at all? — money as circulation rather than possession, the tradition of giving at Diwali, and Lakshmi seated on a lotus that rises clean out of muddy water
Close: This week, move one thing along, a donation, a returned favour, a cleared drawer; the old idea is that fortune enters where there is room.
takeaways: Lakshmi is called Chanchala, restless, because in Hindu stories wealth never stays where it is disrespected or hoarded.
The Vishnu Purana tells how she left Indra's heaven after he insulted the sage Durvasa, and returned only through the churning of the ocean.
Folk tradition adds her sister Alakshmi, who follows neglect and quarrels, a reminder about the conditions in which prosperity stays.

faq.q: What does Chanchala Lakshmi mean?
faq.a: Chanchala means restless, fickle or moving. Applied to Lakshmi, it expresses the traditional understanding that wealth and fortune are not permanent possessions. They come and go, and the stories say she stays only where there is effort, order, generosity and respect. It is less a criticism of the goddess than an honest observation about money.

faq.q: Who are Lakshmi and Alakshmi?
faq.a: In folk tradition, Alakshmi is Lakshmi's elder sister, sometimes linked with Jyeshtha, who is said to have emerged from the churning of the ocean before her. Where Lakshmi brings prosperity and harmony, Alakshmi is associated with poverty, quarrels and neglect. Cleaning the home and lighting lamps before worshipping Lakshmi is often explained as keeping Alakshmi away.

faq.q: What is the story of Durvasa's curse on Indra?
faq.a: In the Vishnu Purana, the sage Durvasa gave Indra a sacred garland. Indra placed it on his elephant Airavata, which tossed it to the ground. Insulted, Durvasa cursed Indra and the gods to lose their fortune. Lakshmi withdrew from heaven, and the gods had to churn the ocean with the asuras to bring her back.

posts.title: Honesty in Business: Lessons From a Kumbakonam Shop
posts.description: Honesty in business, Hinduism's way, learned in my Thatha's Kumbakonam cloth shop: the true measure, the first sale, and what it means in a US office.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: My Thatha measured cloth with a wooden rod worn smooth at one end, and he never let the fabric stretch under his thumb; that was the whole of his business philosophy, and he never called it one.
## The Kumbakonam counter — the lamp lit before the shutters opened, the first sale of the morning treated as a small blessing, the customer told plainly that a dye would run

## Is honesty in business Hinduism's idea or just good sense? — satya as a daily practice rather than a doctrine, the Tirukkural on trade, and why Thatha said an honest shop and a busy shop take the same number of years to build
## A New Jersey version of the measuring rod — a sales call where rounding up would be easy, a vendor's gift, a colleague who needs credit for their work; small choices that no one sees
Close: One thing to carry into the week: before you send the number, the estimate or the promise, measure it once more without your thumb on the cloth.
takeaways: Honesty in business, in the Hindu view, is satya practised daily: a true measure, a plain word about a flaw, a promise kept.
A small Kumbakonam cloth shop taught what the Tirukkural says about trade: guard the customer's interest as your own.
The same test works in a US office: would you be comfortable if the other person could see exactly how you measured?

faq.q: What are Hindu values at work?
faq.a: Many Hindus draw on ideas such as satya, truthfulness; ahimsa, avoiding harm; seva, service; and doing one's duty without clinging to the result, as the Bhagavad Gita teaches. At work, that can mean honest reporting, fair treatment of colleagues, giving credit where it is due and doing a task well even when no one is watching.

faq.q: What does honest measure in trade mean in Hinduism?
faq.a: Honest measure means giving exactly what the customer pays for, with true weights, lengths and descriptions. Dharmashastra texts list false weights among the serious wrongs of a trader, and the Tirukkural praises impartiality like a level balance. In daily life it extends to honest estimates, accurate invoices and not hiding a product's defects.

faq.q: How does satya apply in business?
faq.a: Satya means truth, and in Hindu ethics it covers both honest speech and alignment between word and action. In business, that means making claims you can stand behind, keeping commitments, and correcting mistakes openly. The tradition also values speaking truth kindly, so satya is not bluntness; it is reliability that other people can build on.

posts.title: Ishta Devata Meaning: Choosing Your Own God
posts.description: Ishta devata meaning explained: why Hindus may choose a personal form of God, how it differs from the family deity, and gentle ways people find their own.
posts.author: hariharan
secondaryKeywords: how to find your ishta devata
outline: Hook: Hinduism lets you choose which face of the divine you turn to, and nobody thinks that strange; the idea has a name, ishta devata, the beloved or chosen deity.

## Ishta devata meaning — ishta as desired or beloved, devata as deity; the form to which your heart naturally goes; the seventh chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says he steadies the faith of each worshipper in whatever form they approach
## How is it different from a kula devata? — the family deity inherited through lineage and the temple the family returns to, alongside the deity a person chooses; both can be honoured at once

## How do people find their own? — the panchayatana puja of five deities with one at the centre, a pull felt at a particular temple, a story that stays with you; stories told in many families, not a test to pass
Close: If you have no ishta devata yet, simply notice which story you keep returning to, and give that form a lamp for a week.
takeaways: Ishta devata means the beloved or chosen deity, the particular form of the divine a person feels most drawn to.
It differs from the kula devata, the family deity inherited through lineage; many Hindus honour both.
Traditions such as panchayatana puja let a worshipper place their chosen deity at the centre while honouring others around it.

faq.q: What is the difference between ishta devata and kula devata?
faq.a: The kula devata is the family or clan deity, inherited through one's lineage and often tied to an ancestral village temple. The ishta devata is the personal, chosen form of the divine a person feels closest to. They may be the same or different. Many families visit the kula devata temple for key events while each member worships their own ishta devata.

faq.q: How do I find my ishta devata?
faq.a: There is no single method. Many people simply notice which form of the divine they feel drawn to, through a temple visit, a story, a mantra that moves them or a family tradition. Some ask a guru or elder for guidance. Others use a Jyotish reading as one input. Give the connection time; it often becomes clear gradually rather than all at once.

faq.q: What is panchayatana puja?
faq.a: Panchayatana puja is the worship of five deities together, usually Shiva, Vishnu, Devi, Surya and Ganesha, arranged with the worshipper's chosen deity at the centre and the other four around it. The practice is traditionally associated with Adi Shankaracharya and the Smarta tradition. It expresses the idea that one divine reality can be approached through many forms.

posts.title: Ekam Sat: Many Paths, One Truth in the Rig Veda
posts.description: Ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti, read in its Rig Veda setting: what the line says about one truth and many names, and what it does and does not claim.
posts.author: hariharan
secondaryKeywords: truth is one sages call it by many names
outline: Hook: Truth is one; the wise call it by many names. It is the most quoted line in Hinduism, and it is worth reading the verse around it before quoting it again.

## What does ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti actually say? — Rig Veda 1.164.46, in the long riddle hymn attributed to Dirghatamas: they call it Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, the winged Garutman, Yama, Matarishvan; one being, many names

## Does it mean all religions are the same? — the verse is about names of Vedic deities, not a modern declaration; how later thinkers, from Vedanta teachers to Vivekananda, widened it; honest about both the original and the reading
## Why has the line lasted? — the riddle hymn's habit of asking rather than asserting, and a tradition that kept many paths, schools and deities without insisting they collapse into one
Close: Next time the line comes up, try saying it as a question as well as an answer; the hymn it comes from would approve.
takeaways: Ekam sat vipra bahudha vadanti, from Rig Veda 1.164.46, means truth is one, but the wise speak of it in many ways.
In context, the verse says Indra, Agni, Varuna and others are names for one reality; it is not a statement about modern world religions.
Later Hindu thinkers widened it into a principle of openness, which is why it is quoted so often today.

faq.q: What is the ekam sat meaning?
faq.a: Ekam sat means that which is, is one. The full line from the Rig Veda continues vipra bahudha vadanti, the wise speak of it in many ways. It expresses the idea that a single reality lies behind the many names used for the divine, which later Hindu philosophy developed in schools such as Vedanta.

faq.q: Where does 'truth is one, sages call it by many names' come from?
faq.a: The phrase is a popular translation of Rig Veda 1.164.46, part of a long hymn of riddles traditionally attributed to the seer Dirghatamas. The verse lists Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Agni, Garutman, Yama and Matarishvan as names the wise use for the one reality. Translations vary slightly, but the core meaning is widely agreed.

faq.q: Does ekam sat mean all religions are equal?
faq.a: Not in its original setting. The verse speaks of Vedic deities as names of one reality. Modern teachers extended the principle to other faiths as an expression of openness, and many Hindus hold that view sincerely. Others read it more narrowly. Both readings are common, and it helps to know which one someone means.

posts.title: Shastrartha: Why Hindu Texts Love a Good Debate
posts.description: Shastrartha debate in Hinduism: why texts love argument, from Nachiketa and Yama to Shankara and Mandana Mishra, and the rule of stating the rival view first.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: In many Hindu texts, the holiest thing a student can do is ask an awkward question and refuse to accept the first answer; argument is not the opposite of devotion, it is one of its forms.

## How did shastrartha debate work in Hinduism? — shastrartha as debate on the meaning of the texts; the purvapaksha rule of stating your opponent's view fairly before answering it; Nyaya's distinction between honest inquiry, debate to win and mere fault-finding

## The famous debates — Nachiketa refusing Yama's bribes in the Katha Upanishad, and the tradition in the Shankara Digvijaya of Shankara debating Mandana Mishra with Ubhaya Bharati as judge and garlands that would wilt on the loser
## Why argue with God? — Arjuna questioning Krishna for eighteen chapters, and a tradition that preserved the positions it rejected so the next student could test them
Close: In your next disagreement, try the purvapaksha habit: state the other person's view well enough that they nod before you answer.
takeaways: Shastrartha is formal debate on the meaning of sacred texts, and Hindu tradition treats it as a serious, even devotional, way of seeking truth.
Its core discipline is purvapaksha: stating an opposing view fairly and fully before replying.
Stories like Nachiketa and Yama, or Shankara and Mandana Mishra, show questioning honoured, not punished.

faq.q: What does purvapaksha mean?
faq.a: Purvapaksha means the prior position, the view of the opponent. In Indian philosophical writing, an author first states the opposing argument as strongly and fairly as possible, then responds with the siddhanta, the established conclusion. The method forces a thinker to understand the other side before refuting it, and it runs through Vedanta, Mimamsa and Nyaya texts.

faq.q: What happened in the Shankara and Mandana Mishra debate?
faq.a: According to the Shankara Digvijaya, a traditional biography, the young Adi Shankaracharya debated the ritualist scholar Mandana Mishra for many days. Mandana's learned wife, Ubhaya Bharati, served as judge and placed a garland on each; the one whose garland wilted first would lose. Mandana's faded, and he became Shankara's disciple. Historians treat the account as hagiography.

faq.q: What are vada, jalpa and vitanda?
faq.a: The Nyaya school distinguishes three kinds of debate. Vada is honest discussion aimed at truth, with both sides open to correction. Jalpa is debate aimed at winning, using any clever argument. Vitanda only attacks the other view without defending one's own. Nyaya texts praise vada and treat the other two as lesser forms.

posts.title: The Four Ashramas: The Household and the Forest
posts.description: The four ashramas of life explained through a story: the proud ascetic sent to learn dharma from a butcher, and why the household was never second best.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: A forest ascetic burned a bird with an angry glance and felt very holy about it; then a housewife and a butcher taught him what holiness looked like. The four ashramas start there.

## What are the four ashramas of life? — brahmacharya the student, grihastha the householder, vanaprastha the forest dweller, sannyasa the renunciant; as the Dharmasutras and later dharmashastras describe them, an ideal pattern more than a rule everyone lived

## The Vyadha Gita: dharma learned from a butcher — the Mahabharata's Vana Parva story of Kaushika, the housewife who knew about the crane, and Dharmavyadha in Mithila, who taught duty, care for parents and honest work

## Is the forest better than the house? — the Mahabharata's praise of the householder as the one who supports all the others, King Janaka ruling while unattached, and vanaprastha as loosening rather than leaving
Close: Wherever you are in life, student, parent or retiree, ask what this stage asks of you, rather than which stage would look more spiritual.
takeaways: The four ashramas are the traditional stages of life: student, householder, forest dweller and renunciant, each with its own duties.
The texts often praise the householder as the stage that supports all others, not a lesser path.
In the Mahabharata's Vyadha Gita, a proud ascetic learns dharma from a housewife and a butcher, a reminder that holiness is found in ordinary duty.

faq.q: What does vanaprastha mean?
faq.a: Vanaprastha literally means going to the forest. It is the third of the four ashramas, traditionally begun when one's children are grown. The householder gradually hands over responsibilities, simplifies life and turns more toward study and spiritual practice. Today many Hindus interpret it as a gentle stepping back in later life rather than literally moving to a forest.

faq.q: What are the duties of the grihastha ashrama?
faq.a: The grihastha, or householder, earns a living honestly, raises a family, cares for parents, welcomes guests, supports teachers and renunciants, and performs daily worship and charity. Texts describe the householder as the foundation that sustains every other stage of life. Pursuing wealth and pleasure is permitted here, but always within dharma.

faq.q: What is the Vyadha Gita story?
faq.a: In the Mahabharata's Vana Parva, the ascetic Kaushika kills a crane with an angry look, then is rebuked by a housewife who knows what he did. She sends him to Dharmavyadha, a meat seller in Mithila, who teaches him that dharma lies in caring for one's parents, honest work and self-restraint, not in dramatic austerity alone.

posts.title: Who Was Thiruvalluvar? The Poet Behind the Kural
posts.description: Who was Thiruvalluvar? Legend calls him a weaver of Mylapore and scholars disagree on his dates. What we know, what we guess, and why the Kural outlived him.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: We know almost nothing certain about the man who wrote 1330 couplets on how to live; the story says he was a weaver in Mylapore, and the story is really about how a book can be bigger than its author.
## Who was Thiruvalluvar, as far as anyone knows? — the name Valluvar and what it may signal; dates that scholars place centuries apart with no agreement, which is why no years are given here

## The legends: a loom, a wife named Vasuki, a plank that shrank — popular stories of the Mylapore weaver, Vasuki's patience, the later tale of the Madurai Sangam plank that made room only for the Kural; what the legends say about wisdom growing out of household life

## Why does every faith claim the Kural? — no sectarian god is named; the first kural, 'Agara mudhala', compares the Primal God to the letter A, first of all letters; Jain, Shaiva, Vaishnava and secular readers all find themselves in it
Close: A gentle reframe — perhaps the anonymity is the gift; the Kural asks to be judged by what it says, not by who said it
takeaways: Thiruvalluvar was the Tamil poet who wrote the Tirukkural, 1330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love; his dates are uncertain and scholars disagree by centuries.
Most of his biography is legend, including the Mylapore weaver and his wife Vasuki; what survives with certainty is the book itself.

faq.q: When did Thiruvalluvar live?
faq.a: Nobody knows for certain. Scholars have proposed dates that differ by several centuries, based on the language of the Kural, its ideas and the later Tamil works that quote it. Tradition does not settle the question either. The honest answer is that he belongs to the classical period of Tamil literature, and the book is far better documented than the man.

faq.q: Was Thiruvalluvar Hindu, Jain or something else?
faq.a: Many traditions claim him. Shaiva, Vaishnava and Jain readers each find their own ideas in the Kural, and the text itself names no sectarian deity. Its opening compares the Primal God to the letter A, which leaves room for many readings. That openness is one reason the Tirukkural is read and respected by Tamils of every faith and of none.

faq.q: Is the story of Thiruvalluvar and Vasuki true?
faq.a: It is a much-loved legend rather than recorded thiruvalluvar history. Popular stories describe him as a weaver in Mylapore, now part of Chennai, married to Vasuki, a wife of legendary patience and devotion. The stories are told to show that his wisdom grew out of ordinary household life. There is no contemporary record, so treat them as meaningful tradition, not biography.

posts.title: Tirukkural for Daily Life: A Beginner's Way In
posts.description: Thirukkural for daily life, the NRI way: one couplet a day on the train, the three books in plain English, and how a Tamil classic fits a New Jersey week.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: The easiest way into the Tirukkural is one couplet a day; I started reading one on the train out of Edison, and the two lines lasted longer than the ride.
## What is in the Kural, in one minute? — 133 chapters of ten couplets each, 1330 in all, in three books: Aram (virtue), Porul (wealth and public life) and Inbam (love)

## Thirukkural for daily life: a one-couplet method — read one kural in Tamil and in an English rendering, carry one phrase through the day, notice where it turns up (a meeting, a queue, a call home); start with Iniyavai Kooral (Pleasant Words) or Seynandri Arithal (Gratitude)

## Reading it with a child in America — reading aloud with my son, choosing a chapter together, letting him argue with Valluvar; the Kural's secular tone makes it easy to share with friends of any faith
Close: One small thing for the week — pick one chapter, read one couplet each morning for seven days, and say one line aloud at dinner
takeaways: The simplest way to use the Tirukkural daily is to read one couplet each morning and carry a single phrase with you through the day.
Its 1330 couplets sit in three books, on virtue, wealth and love, so you can begin with whichever part of life feels most pressing.

faq.q: How do I start reading Thirukkural as a beginner?
faq.a: Start small. Choose one chapter, such as Iniyavai Kooral on pleasant words, and read one couplet a day in Tamil and in a trusted English translation. Read it aloud once, then carry a single phrase with you. Ten days finishes a chapter. You will learn more from living with ten couplets than from rushing through a hundred.

faq.q: Is there a good way to read Thirukkural in English?
faq.a: Yes. Several respected English translations exist, and many editions print the Tamil couplet, a transliteration and the English side by side. Try two translations of the same kural to see how much meaning sits in each word. If you do not read Tamil script, listen to the couplet recited aloud so that its rhythm stays with you.

faq.q: Can non-Tamils or people of other faiths read the Tirukkural?
faq.a: Absolutely. The Tirukkural is ethical rather than sectarian, and people of many faiths and none have read it for centuries. It speaks about honesty, patience, friendship, work and love in terms anyone can test in daily life. That is why it travels so well, from a Chennai classroom to a commuter train in New Jersey.

posts.title: Tirukkural on Wealth: Earning Without Losing Yourself
posts.description: Thirukkural on wealth, seen from my Thatha's cloth shop in Kumbakonam: the Porul section on earning honestly, spending wisely and giving without display.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: The Tirukkural treats wealth as necessary, not shameful; my Thatha ran his cloth shop in Kumbakonam as if he had read the Porul section closely, and perhaps he had.

## What does the Porul section actually say about money? — Porul, the second and longest book, covers wealth, statecraft and public life; the chapter Porul Seyalvagai (Ways of Earning Wealth) on wealth as a means to good ends; elsewhere the Kural warns that wealth won through others' tears leaves with tears

## Thirukkural on wealth at Thatha's counter — measuring cloth honestly, extending credit to weavers in a bad season, closing the shop for a neighbour's funeral; wealth in the Kural includes reputation and trust

## Earning in America without losing yourself — the salary, the remittance home, the pull to keep score; wealth as a means to Aram (virtue) and to giving, as in the chapter Oppuravu Arithal (Duty to Society)
Close: One small thing for the week — before one purchase or one transfer home, ask Thatha's question: was this earned cleanly, and will it help someone?
takeaways: The Tirukkural does not despise wealth; its Porul section treats honest earning as a duty that supports virtue, family and society.
Valluvar's test is how money is made and used: wealth gained through harm brings sorrow, while wealth shared quietly sustains the giver.

faq.q: What does Thirukkural say about money?
faq.a: The Tirukkural treats money as essential for a good life, not as something to renounce. Its second book, Porul, discusses earning, managing and protecting wealth, and praises wealth gained by fair means. It is equally clear that riches won through deceit or harm do not last and bring grief. The measure is always the means and the use.

faq.q: What is the meaning of Porul in the Thirukkural?
faq.a: Porul means wealth or material concerns, and it names the second of the Tirukkural's three books, between Aram (virtue) and Inbam (love). It is the longest book and covers rulers, ministers, friendship, the economy of households and kingdoms, and conduct in public life. Readers today often turn to it for wisdom on leadership, business and careers.

faq.q: Is it wrong to want wealth in Hindu and Tamil tradition?
faq.a: No. Both the Tamil ethical tradition and the wider Hindu idea of the purusharthas treat wealth, artha, as a legitimate aim of life. The Tirukkural simply insists that it be earned without harming others and used for family, guests and people in need. Wanting a secure income is ordinary; forgetting how it was earned is what the text warns against.

posts.title: Tirukkural on Anger: The Fire That Burns the Holder
posts.description: Thirukkural on anger, from a stalled commute: the Vegulamai chapter says anger burns the one who holds it. What Valluvar meant, and one small practice.
posts.author: manikandan
secondaryKeywords: how to control anger tamil wisdom
outline: Hook: The Tirukkural's chapter on anger says the fire you nurse destroys you first; I remembered that one morning, stuck on the Turnpike, knuckles white on the wheel.

## Vegulamai (Not Being Angry): what the chapter covers — ten couplets in the book of virtue on restraining anger, above all toward those weaker than you; anger as a fire that harms the one who kindles it and even the circle of kin around them

## Thirukkural on anger at a red light — the driver who cut in, the email waiting at work; how anger aimed at people who cannot answer back (a junior colleague, a child) is exactly what Valluvar singles out
## Is all anger wrong in the Kural? — the flash versus the grudge; the counsel to forget anger toward anyone; anger as the thing that kills laughter and joy
Close: One small thing for the week — when anger rises in traffic or in a meeting, wait three breaths before speaking, and notice who would have paid for the words
takeaways: The Tirukkural's Vegulamai chapter teaches that anger harms its holder first, burning relationships and peace before it touches anyone else.
Valluvar is especially firm about anger toward those who cannot answer back; restraint matters most where you hold the power.

faq.q: What does vegulamai mean in the Thirukkural?
faq.a: Vegulamai means not being angry, or the restraint of anger. It is the name of a ten-couplet chapter in Aram, the Tirukkural's book of virtue. The chapter asks the reader to forget anger toward anyone, warns that anger destroys laughter and joy, and pictures anger as a fire that harms the person who holds it and those close to them.

faq.q: Is it okay to feel angry according to Hindu teachings?
faq.a: Feeling anger is human, and the traditions do not pretend otherwise. The Bhagavad Gita cautions against being ruled by it, tracing a chain from desire to anger to confusion, and the Tirukkural, read by people of every faith, makes a similar point. The practical teaching is to notice anger early, delay the words or actions, and let the heat pass before it hardens into a grudge.

faq.q: Are there Thirukkural quotes on anger I can remember?
faq.a: The easiest to remember is the chapter's central image: anger is a fire that burns the one who kindles it, and even the circle of family around them. Another idea worth carrying is that restraining anger matters most where you have the power to hurt. Read the Vegulamai chapter slowly, one couplet a day, and keep the line that fits your temper.

posts.title: Tirukkural on Kind Words: Why Sweet Speech Matters

posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: The Tirukkural says choosing a harsh word when a kind one is available is like picking unripe fruit when ripe fruit hangs within reach; I thought of it in a Monday meeting that went sideways.

## Iniyavai Kooral (Pleasant Words): what the chapter asks — speech that is loving, free of deceit and true, spoken with a cheerful face; why Valluvar places it in the book of virtue, right after the chapter on hospitality

## Thirukkural on speech in a meeting room — the project that slipped, the colleague who took the blame, the email I almost sent; sweet speech is not flattery but choosing the ripe fruit of the same truth
## Does kind speech mean never saying hard things? — the Kural pairs sweetness with truth; honest feedback can be ripe or raw, and the difference is timing, tone and intent
Close: One small thing for the week — before one difficult message, rewrite the first sentence so it would be easy to hear, then send it
takeaways: The Tirukkural's Iniyavai Kooral chapter teaches that kind words cost nothing, while choosing harsh words over kind ones is like picking unripe fruit.
Sweet speech in the Kural is not flattery; it is the same truth, offered at the right time and in a tone the listener can receive.

faq.q: What does iniyavai kooral mean?
faq.a: Iniyavai Kooral means speaking pleasant words. It is a ten-couplet chapter in the Tirukkural's book of virtue. Valluvar describes kind speech as words that are loving, free of deceit and true, spoken with a pleasant face. Its best-known image compares harsh speech to choosing unripe fruit when ripe fruit is right there to pick.

faq.q: What is the ripe fruit and unripe fruit kural about?
faq.a: It is the closing couplet of the Iniyavai Kooral chapter. Valluvar asks why anyone would speak harsh words when sweet words are available, comparing it to plucking unripe fruit while ripe fruit hangs within reach. The point is practical: kind speech is always an option, it costs nothing, and the harsh version rarely achieves more.

faq.q: How can I practise kind speech at work?
faq.a: Start with the first sentence. Most difficult messages go wrong in the opening line, so rewrite it until it would be easy to hear, while keeping the facts intact. Give feedback in private, name the problem rather than the person, and pause before replying when you feel stung. Kind speech at work is a habit of small choices, repeated daily.

## Seynandri Arithal (Gratitude): what the chapter says — help given unasked, help given in time, help given without calculation; a small kindness at the right moment outweighs the world

## Thirukkural on gratitude across an ocean — the parents who paid for college, the neighbour who drove my mother to the hospital, my first manager in New Jersey; gratitude as remembering, not repaying

## Why does Valluvar call ingratitude the hardest failing to undo? — the chapter's closing idea that other lapses have a way out and forgetting kindness does not; read gently, as encouragement rather than threat
Close: One small thing for the week — name one person whose help you never repaid, and tell them, or tell someone about them
takeaways: The Tirukkural's Seynandri Arithal chapter teaches that help given when nothing was owed is beyond repayment, so the right response is lifelong remembrance.
Valluvar values timely help most: a small kindness at the right moment is, in his words, larger than the world.

faq.q: What does seynandri arithal mean?
faq.a: Seynandri Arithal means knowing, or acknowledging, the help one has received. It is the Tirukkural chapter on gratitude, in the book of virtue. Its ten couplets say that unasked help cannot be repaid even with earth and heaven, that timely help outweighs the world however small it looks, and that forgetting a kindness is the hardest failing to undo.

faq.q: Is there a kural about thankfulness I can share with family?
faq.a: The opening couplet of the gratitude chapter is a good one to share. It says that help given without any earlier favour to repay is so great that even earth and heaven together could not match it. Many families read it at birthdays or anniversaries as a way of thanking parents and elders without a long speech.

faq.q: How do I show gratitude to parents who live far away?
faq.a: Gratitude travels well in small, regular forms. A fixed weekly call, remembering their medical appointments, sending their favourite sweets at a festival or arranging a pooja on their star birthday all say thank you. Tell them specific memories of what they did for you. PariharaOnline can help with a pooja in their name, but the remembering matters most.

## Natpu (Friendship): what Valluvar asks of a friend — a group of chapters in the Porul book on friendship, testing friends and false friends; the friend who steadies you before embarrassment spreads
## Thirukkural on friendship at the shop counter — Thatha's friend the weaver, a lean season, credit extended without a word; friendship as reflex, not transaction

## How do you test a friend, according to the Kural? — Valluvar's counsel to examine before befriending, since a friendship once made is hard to leave; misfortune as the measuring rod that shows who stays
Close: One small thing for the week — call one friend who once caught your slipping cloth, and tell them you remember
takeaways: The Tirukkural compares true friendship to a hand that instantly catches a slipping garment: help given as reflex, before shame can spread.
Valluvar advises examining a person before making them a friend, and notes that hard times are the truest measure of friendship.

faq.q: What does Thirukkural say about true friends?
faq.a: Valluvar devotes several chapters of the Porul book to friendship. A true friend, he says, acts at once when you stumble, like a hand catching a garment that slips, and corrects you when you go wrong. He warns against friends who are sweet in words but absent in action, and suggests that misfortune reveals who your real friends are.

faq.q: What is the natpu adhikaram meaning?
faq.a: Natpu is the Tamil word for friendship, and an adhikaram is a chapter of the Tirukkural. Natpu is a ten-couplet chapter in the Porul book, followed by related chapters on examining friendship, long-standing friendship, bad friendship and false friendship. Together they form one of the fullest treatments of friendship in any classical text.

faq.q: How can I be a better friend as an adult with little time?
faq.a: Friendship in adult life runs on small reliable acts rather than long hours. Reply when a friend is struggling, show up for the hard occasions such as a hospital visit or a funeral, and say the uncomfortable truth kindly when it is needed. The Kural's image of the hand catching the cloth is about speed and instinct, not grand gestures.

posts.title: Tirukkural on Learning: Kalvi and the Lifelong Student
posts.description: Thirukkural on education: the Kalvi chapter calls learning the one wealth that cannot be lost, and says knowledge deepens like a sand well as you dig.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: The Tirukkural says the learned keep learning the way a well dug in sand keeps giving water the deeper you go; learning, in Valluvar's hands, is really about never reaching the bottom.
## Kalvi (Learning): what the chapter says — learn thoroughly and then live by it; numbers and letters as the two eyes of every living person; learning as the one wealth that does not decay

## Thirukkural on education: the sand well and the digging — why Valluvar chose a well scooped in a riverbed, the patience it implies, and the companion chapter Kelvi (Listening), which treats hearing the wise as learning too

## Why does the Kural call learning wealth? — in a book full of kings and treasuries, learning is the treasure no thief, fire or flood can take; how this sits beside Saraswati worship and Vidyarambham without belonging to any one sect
Close: A gentle reframe — a student is not someone young, but someone still digging
takeaways: The Tirukkural's Kalvi chapter calls learning the only imperishable wealth and says knowledge grows the way water rises in a sand well dug deeper.
Valluvar asks for learning that is thorough and then lived, treating numbers and letters as the two eyes of every person.

faq.q: What is the meaning of the Kalvi adhikaram in Thirukkural?
faq.a: Kalvi means learning, and this ten-couplet adhikaram, or chapter, in the Porul book urges people to learn thoroughly and then act on what they learn. It calls numbers and letters the two eyes of a living being, compares growing knowledge to a sand well that yields more water the deeper it is dug, and calls learning the one wealth that never decays.

faq.q: Why does Thiruvalluvar say learning is the best wealth?
faq.a: Because it cannot be taken away. Land, gold and position can be lost to thieves, floods, rulers or bad luck, but learning stays with the learner and even grows when shared. The closing thought of the Kalvi chapter is that learning is imperishable wealth, and that other riches do not deserve the name by comparison.

faq.q: Is the Thirukkural still relevant to education today?
faq.a: Many teachers think so. Its ideas are practical: learn deeply rather than widely and shallowly, listen to people who know more than you, keep learning throughout life and let learning shape conduct. Tamil schools teach its couplets to children, and adults return to them through careers and retirement. The sand well image suits a lifelong student of any age.

## Thirukkural on patience in a recovery room — video calls during physiotherapy, my father snapping at my mother, my own temper over a bad connection; forbearance as the quiet work of the people around the sick

Valluvar says forgiving a wrong is good and forgetting it is better; forbearance is presented as strength, not weakness.

faq.q: What does poraiyudaimai mean?
faq.a: Poraiyudaimai means possessing forbearance, the capacity to bear wrongs and harsh words without striking back. It is a ten-couplet chapter in the Tirukkural's book of virtue. Its opening image is the earth, which supports even those who dig into it. The chapter also teaches that forgiving an injury is good and forgetting it entirely is better still.

faq.q: Does forbearance in the Tirukkural mean tolerating abuse?
faq.a: No. Forbearance in the Tirukkural is about not retaliating and not nursing grudges, which protects your own peace. It is not an instruction to remain in danger or accept mistreatment. You can leave a harmful situation, seek help and set firm boundaries while still refusing to answer cruelty with cruelty. Valluvar presents restraint as strength, freely chosen.

faq.q: How can I become more patient with family?

Keep one steady routine, such as a weekly call at a fixed time, so conversations are not squeezed into stressful moments. Forgive quickly, and let minor things go unmentioned.

faq.q: What does virunthombal mean in the Thirukkural?
faq.a: Virunthombal means cherishing guests. It is an early chapter in the Tirukkural's book of virtue, with ten couplets on hospitality. faq.q: What is the meaning of atithi devo bhava?
faq.a: Atithi devo bhava is a Sanskrit phrase from the Taittiriya Upanishad, usually translated as the guest is like God. It captures a wide Indian ideal: receiving a visitor with the care and respect you would offer the divine, whether the visit was expected or not.

faq.q: How do I host guests well when I am short on time?

Keep one simple dish you can make quickly, such as upma or lemon rice. Guests remember how they were received far longer than what they ate.

faq.q: What does anbudaimai mean?

faq.q: What is anbu in the Thirukkural?

faq.q: What does aalvinaiyudaimai mean?
faq.a: Aalvinaiyudaimai means possessing manly effort, or perseverance. It is a ten-couplet chapter in the Porul book of the Tirukkural. Valluvar says that effort, not luck, builds a person's worth, that idleness is the real misfortune, and that even when destiny refuses success, sincere labour still yields its reward. Its final couplet speaks of persistent people turning fate back.

faq.q: What does Thirukkural say about perseverance?
faq.a: The Tirukkural treats perseverance as one of the most dependable virtues. It advises against dropping a task because it looks difficult, warns that the world leaves behind those who leave work unfinished, and promises that persistent effort pays even when circumstances are against you. Valluvar's tone is encouraging rather than stern: keep going, and the effort itself will count.

faq.q: Does Hinduism favour fate or effort?
faq.a: Both, held together. Hindu and Tamil traditions accept that some things are shaped by past karma or destiny, yet they insist that present effort matters. faq.q: When is Ugadi celebrated?
faq.a: Ugadi falls on the first day of the bright half of the lunar month of Chaitra, the day after the new moon, which usually lands in March or April. Because it follows the lunar calendar, the date moves each year. Check the current year's panchangam or your local temple's calendar for the exact day and the auspicious time for the morning puja.

faq.q: Why is Ugadi celebrated?
faq.a: Ugadi is celebrated as the start of a new lunar year. Tradition holds that Brahma began creating the world on this day, so it is treated as a fresh beginning for the household. Families clean the home, hang mango-leaf torans, wear new clothes, pray, eat the six-taste Ugadi pachadi and listen to the new year's panchangam being read aloud.

faq.q: What is the story of Brahma and Ugadi?
faq.a: The ugadi story most families tell is that Brahma, the creator, began the work of creation on the first day of Chaitra, which is why time is counted afresh from this morning. The name itself joins yuga, an age, and adi, a beginning. The story frames the new year as creation starting again, with the household invited to begin with it.

faq.q: Is Ugadi the same as Gudi Padwa?
faq.a: They fall on the same day and share the idea of a lunar new year. Ugadi is the Telugu and Kannada name; Gudi Padwa is the Marathi celebration, where families raise a gudi, a decorated pole topped with an upturned pot, at the doorway. Customs and foods differ by region, but the meaning of a fresh start is common to both.

faq.q: When is Tamil New Year celebrated?

faq.q: Is Puthandu the same as Vishu or Ugadi?

Its significance is strength in service: Hanuman's power is remembered not for itself but for what he did for Rama and Sita.

faq.q: Why is Hanuman Jayanti celebrated on different dates?
faq.a: Regional calendars mark Hanuman's birth differently. Much of North India observes it on the full moon of Chaitra, in March or April. Tamil Nadu observes Hanumath Jayanthi on the new moon of Margazhi, in December or January, traditionally linked with the Mula star. Andhra, Telangana and Karnataka traditions keep other dates. Follow your family's custom and check the local panchangam.

faq.q: What is the story of Hanuman forgetting his powers?
faq.a: In the Ramayana tradition, young Hanuman's pranks disturbed sages in the forest, who laid a curse that he would forget his strength until someone reminded him. In the Kishkindha Kanda, as the monkeys despair on the shore facing the ocean, the old bear Jambavan recounts Hanuman's birth and power. Remembering, Hanuman grows and leaps across the sea to Lanka.

faq.q: Why is Hanuman Jayanti celebrated?
faq.a: Families celebrate Hanuman Jayanti to honour Hanuman's birth and the qualities he stands for: courage, loyalty, humility and tireless service to Rama. Devotees visit temples, offer vadai garlands, betel leaves, butter or sindoor depending on region, and read the Hanuman Chalisa or Sundara Kanda. posts.title: Akshaya Tritiya Significance: What Never Runs Out
posts.description: Akshaya Tritiya significance: the stories of Sudama's rice, the Akshaya Patra and Parashurama, and why giving, not only buying gold, is the heart of the day.
posts.author: hariharan

outline: Hook: A poor Brahmin walks to Dwaraka with a handful of beaten rice tied in a cloth, too ashamed to offer it. Krishna eats it with joy. The story is about a gift so small it was nearly hidden, and a day named for what never runs out.

## Akshaya Tritiya significance: what 'akshaya' means — the third day of the bright half of Vaishakha, usually April or May; akshaya as that which does not diminish; the belief that what you begin or give today keeps growing

## Which stories belong to this day? — Sudama and the aval; the Akshaya Patra given to the Pandavas in exile so no guest went hungry; Parashurama's birth; the tradition that Vyasa began dictating the Mahabharata to Ganesha

## Gold, or giving? — how buying gold became the modern custom; the older practice of dana: water pots, fans, umbrellas and food in the summer heat; the story is really about the vessel, not what it holds
Close: the Akshaya Patra fed everyone until Draupadi herself had eaten; on this day, feed someone before you buy anything.
takeaways: Akshaya Tritiya falls on the third day of the bright half of Vaishakha; akshaya means never diminishing, and the day is believed to make good beginnings and gifts last.
Its best-loved stories, Sudama's beaten rice and the Pandavas' Akshaya Patra, are about generosity and food, not gold.

faq.q: Why is Akshaya Tritiya celebrated?
faq.a: Akshaya Tritiya is celebrated as a day when good actions are believed to bear lasting fruit, since akshaya means that which does not diminish. Popular tradition links it with Parashurama's birth, Krishna receiving Sudama's beaten rice, and the Akshaya Patra that fed the Pandavas. Families pray to Lakshmi and Vishnu, start new ventures, and give food, water and clothing.

faq.q: What is the Akshaya Tritiya story?
faq.a: Several stories gather around the day. The best known is Sudama, Krishna's poor childhood friend, who brought only a handful of beaten rice to Dwaraka; Krishna received it gladly and Sudama returned home to find his family provided for. Another tells of the sun god giving the exiled Pandavas the Akshaya Patra, a vessel that never ran empty.

faq.q: What to donate on Akshaya Tritiya?
faq.a: Traditional gifts suit the summer season: water in clay pots, buttermilk, fans, umbrellas, footwear, grains, fruit and cooked food. Feeding people, known as annadanam, is considered especially meaningful. Many families also give to a temple or a food programme in their parents' names. Give what you can with a glad heart; the tradition values intention over the size of the gift.

faq.q: Is buying gold on Akshaya Tritiya necessary?
faq.a: No. Buying gold is a popular modern custom built on the idea that what you acquire today keeps growing. The older emphasis of the day is on dana, giving, and on beginning good work. If you do buy something, many families offer it before the lamp first. Nothing is lost by choosing to give instead of buy.

## Vaikasi Visakam at home, in a small kitchen — a picture or vel, milk or panchamrutham poured slowly, red flowers, a lamp, the Kanda Sashti Kavasam or a few lines of Arunagirinathar's Thiruppugazh, payasam as naivedyam

At home, a lamp, a slow milk abhishekam to a vel or picture, red flowers, payasam and a verse from the Kanda Sashti Kavasam are enough.

faq.q: What is the significance of Vaikasi Visakam?
faq.a: Vaikasi Visakam significance comes from the Kanda Puranam: Murugan was born when six sparks from Shiva's third eye fell into the Saravana pond and became six infants, raised by the Krittika maidens and joined by Parvati into one child with six faces. The day celebrates his birth and his role as the one who removes confusion and fear.

faq.q: How do I do Vaikasi Visakam pooja at home?
faq.a: Clean the puja space and place a picture of Murugan or a small vel. Light a lamp, then pour milk, or panchamrutham, slowly over the vel as abhishekam while chanting 'Om Saravanabhava'. faq.q: When is Vaikasi Visakam celebrated?

The exact day moves each year, so check the current year's panchangam. Murugan temples in India and the US hold special abhishekams and processions.

## What is Chitra Pournami? — the full moon of the Tamil month Chithirai, usually April or May, when the moon is near Chitra star; the brightest night of early summer; girivalam at Tiruvannamalai and the Chithirai festival in Madurai

## Who is Chitragupta, and why does he keep a ledger? — the assistant of Yama who records each person's deeds; the legend of his birth from a drawing, hence 'chitra'; his shrine at Kanchipuram; a record-keeper, not a punisher

## Chitra Pournami at home: moonlight, rice and a review — cooking chitrannam, the variety rices (lemon, tamarind, coconut, curd), eating outdoors under the moon, a lamp, and ten minutes looking honestly at your own ledger
Close: try this for a week from the full moon: each night, before sleep, name one thing you did well and one you would redo. That is the whole practice.
takeaways: Chitra Pournami is the full moon of the Tamil month Chithirai, dedicated in tradition to Chitragupta, who records every person's deeds for Yama.
Families cook variety rices and eat under the moon; the quieter practice is to review your own actions honestly, without fear or guilt.

faq.q: What is the significance of Chitra Pournami?
faq.a: Chitra Pournami significance lies in two things: it is one of the brightest full moons of the year, and it is dedicated to Chitragupta, the keeper of records of every person's good and bad actions. Devotees pray to him for clarity, give food, walk around Arunachala at Tiruvannamalai, and in many homes share a moonlit meal of variety rice.

faq.q: Who is Chitragupta?
faq.a: Chitragupta is the divine accountant who serves Yama, recording each person's deeds. One popular legend says he was created from a picture, a chitra, drawn and brought to life, which is how he got his name. He is honoured especially on Chitra Pournami, and a well-known shrine to him stands in Kanchipuram. Tradition sees him as fair, not fearsome.

faq.q: How do I do Chitra Pournami pooja at home?
faq.a: In the evening, clean the puja space, light a lamp and offer flowers to Chitragupta or to your family deity. Cook chitrannam or a few variety rices, offer them, and eat together outdoors or by a window where you can see the full moon. Some families also place a pen and palm-leaf, or a notebook, before the lamp.

faq.q: When is Chitra Pournami?
faq.a: Chitra Pournami falls on the full moon of the Tamil month Chithirai, which runs from mid-April to mid-May, so it usually comes in late April or May. It is the same full moon that anchors the Chithirai festival in Madurai. The exact date changes each year; check the current year's panchangam.

posts.title: Meenakshi Thirukalyanam: The Wedding a City Attends

## What is Meenakshi Thirukalyanam? — the celestial wedding of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar at the centre of the Chithirai festival, in the Tamil month of Chithirai (April or May); the Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam story of the Pandya princess who ruled, conquered, and met her match on Mount Kailash

## Why does Alagar arrive late? — the story of Meenakshi's brother Kallazhagar setting out from Alagar Kovil to give her away, hearing the wedding is over, and turning back at the Vaigai; what a crowd on a riverbank teaches about showing up anyway

## Keeping the wedding at home — married women renewing the thali thread or manjal kayiru on the day, a lamp and flowers for Meenakshi, watching the temple's live broadcast with parents in India, a small sweet for the family
Close: Manikkavasagar sang of Shiva as the one who came to Madurai for his devotees; this week, go to someone's celebration, even late, even for ten minutes.
takeaways: Meenakshi Thirukalyanam is the divine wedding of Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, the high point of Madurai's Chithirai festival in April or May.
Many married women renew their thali thread on the wedding day, and families far away keep it with a lamp, flowers and the temple broadcast.

faq.q: What is the Chithirai festival in Madurai?
faq.a: The Chithirai festival is Madurai's great spring festival, held over roughly two weeks in the Tamil month of Chithirai. It includes Meenakshi's coronation as queen, her victory procession, the Thirukalyanam or divine wedding with Sundareswarar, a chariot festival, and Kallazhagar's journey from Alagar Kovil to the Vaigai river. It brings together Shaiva and Vaishnava devotion in one city celebration.

faq.q: What is the Meenakshi kalyanam story?
faq.a: The Thiruvilaiyadal Puranam tells of Meenakshi, born to the Pandya king of Madurai, raised as heir and crowned queen. She led her armies to the north and conquered every land until she reached Kailash and saw Shiva, when she recognised him as her husband. Shiva came to Madurai as Sundareswarar, and their wedding is re-enacted every Chithirai.

faq.q: Why does Alagar enter the Vaigai river?
faq.a: In the festival story, Kallazhagar, a form of Vishnu and Meenakshi's brother, sets out from Alagar Kovil to give his sister away. By the time he reaches the Vaigai, the wedding is over, so he enters the river, blesses the devotees and returns. The event, usually near Chitra Pournami, draws enormous crowds to the riverbanks.

faq.q: Can I take part in Meenakshi Thirukalyanam from abroad?
faq.a: Yes. The wedding is widely broadcast, and many families watch it together across time zones, often late at night in the US. At home, light a lamp, offer flowers and a sweet to Meenakshi and Sundareswarar, and married women may renew their thali thread. You can also have an archana done at the temple in your family's names.

## What gives Aadi month significance? — the Tamil month from mid-July to mid-August, the sun entering Karka and the start of Dakshinayana, the monsoon wind; the season when the Goddess is said to come closest to the village

## Fridays, Pooram, Amavasya and Perukku — Aadi Velli pujas to Amman, Aadi Pooram as Andal's birth star and the Goddess's valaikappu with bangles, Aadi Amavasya for the ancestors, Aadi Perukku for the river
Close: the story is really about attention: a month when the calendar sets aside our own plans and turns us toward the Mother. Keep one Friday lamp for her.
takeaways: Aadi, the Tamil month from mid-July to mid-August, is dedicated to the Goddess, with Aadi Fridays, Aadi Pooram, Aadi Amavasya and Aadi Perukku.
Families traditionally avoid weddings and housewarmings in Aadi, a custom explained by farming, monsoon and devotion, not by anything to fear.

faq.q: Why is Aadi month not auspicious for marriage?
faq.a: Tamil families traditionally avoid weddings and housewarmings in Aadi for a mix of reasons. It was the busy sowing season, the monsoon winds made travel hard, and newly married brides customarily spent Aadi at their parents' homes. Many also see the month as reserved for the Goddess rather than household beginnings. It is a custom of timing, not a bad omen.

faq.q: How is Aadi velli pooja done?
faq.a: On each Friday of Aadi, women clean the home, draw a kolam, and light a lamp for the Goddess, often Lakshmi or the local Amman. Many visit an Amman temple, offer koozh, or give bangles and turmeric to married women as thamboolam.

faq.q: What is the significance of Aadi Pooram?
faq.a: Aadi Pooram falls on the day of Pooram star in Aadi and is celebrated as the birth of Andal, the poet-saint of Srivilliputhur, and as a festival of the Goddess. In many Amman temples, the Goddess receives a valaikappu, an offering of bangles like a baby shower, and devotees take the bangles home as prasadam for fertility and family well-being.

faq.q: What is the significance of Aadi Perukku?
faq.a: Aadi Perukku significance is gratitude to water. It falls when the monsoon has filled the Kaveri and other Tamil Nadu rivers just before the sowing season. Families, especially women, go to the riverbank to offer lamps, flowers, turmeric and rice to the river as a mother and a goddess, and pray for a good harvest and a steady household.

faq.q: Why is it called the Aadi 18 festival?
faq.a: Aadi Perukku is also called Padinettam Perukku, the rising of the eighteenth, because it falls on the eighteenth day of the Tamil solar month of Aadi, which usually corresponds to early August. faq.q: How do you do varalakshmi vratham kalasam decoration?

faq.q: What is the Varalakshmi Vratham story?

faq.q: Can I do Varalakshmi pooja on a working day?

faq.q: When is Varalakshmi Vratham?
faq.a: Varalakshmi Vratham falls on the Friday before the full moon of the lunar month Shravana, which usually lands in July or August, in the Tamil months of Aadi or Avani. posts.title: Avani Avittam: Changing the Sacred Thread, Renewing Study

## What is Avani Avittam? — upakarma, the annual renewal of the Vedic student's vow, kept on the full moon of Shravana when the moon is in Avittam in the Tamil month of Avani, usually August; the day varies for Rig, Yajur and Sama Veda families

## Why change the sacred thread? — the yagnopavitam, or poonal, as a vow worn on the body; the old thread set aside, the new one worn with mantras, the Kamo'karshit japa asking pardon for lapses, and the next day's Gayatri japam

## Hayagriva and the return of knowledge — the same full moon as Hayagriva Jayanti, when Vishnu as the horse-headed one restores the stolen Vedas; the day as a festival of learning, not only of a thread
Close: the Taittiriya Upanishad tells the student not to neglect study; this week, pick up one thing you stopped learning and give it fifteen minutes.
takeaways: Avani Avittam is upakarma, the yearly renewal of Vedic study, when those who wear the sacred thread change it with mantras on the full moon of Shravana, usually August.
It shares its full moon with Hayagriva Jayanti, so the day is also a festival of learning and a fresh start for students.

faq.q: What is the significance of Avani Avittam?
faq.a: Avani Avittam significance lies in renewal. It is the day of upakarma, when those initiated into Vedic study renew their commitment, change their sacred thread, and ask forgiveness for lapses over the past year. Traditionally it also marked the start of the Vedic study term. Many families see it as a reminder that learning must be taken up again and again.

faq.q: What does upakarma mean?
faq.a: Upakarma means a beginning or an undertaking, the ceremony that opens a new term of Vedic study. It includes offerings to the rishis who heard the Vedas, the Kamo'karshit japa asking pardon for faults, and wearing a new sacred thread. Different Vedic branches observe it on different days, so Sama Veda families keep it later than Rig and Yajur.

faq.q: How is the poonal changed on Avani Avittam?
faq.a: Changing poonal on Avani Avittam is done after a bath, usually led by a priest or elder at home or at a temple. Participants do sandhyavandanam and sankalpam, offer to the rishis, then wear the new yagnopavitam with its mantra and remove the old one, which is placed in water or under a tree. The next day, many chant the Gayatri mantra over a thousand times.

## What is Naga Panchami significance? — the fifth day of the bright half of Shravana, usually July or August, when the rains drive snakes out of their holes; honouring what we fear instead of killing it; regional variants like Nagula Chavithi and Naga Chathurthi

Close: in almost every one of these stories, the snake is spared. Perhaps that is the festival's quiet instruction: leave the frightening thing alive, and learn to live beside it.
takeaways: Naga Panchami falls on the fifth day of the bright half of Shravana, when families honour snakes with turmeric, flowers and symbolic milk at anthills and stone nagas.
In the stories, from Kaliya to Astika's rescue, snakes are subdued or spared, never exterminated; the festival teaches coexistence with what we fear.

faq.q: Why do we celebrate Naga Panchami?
faq.a: We celebrate Naga Panchami to honour snakes, who appear often during the monsoon and play a role in keeping fields free of pests. Tradition links the day with Astika saving the serpents from Janamejaya's sacrifice and with Krishna sparing Kaliya. Families pray at anthills and naga stones for the protection of children and the household, and to make peace with fear.

faq.q: What is the Naga Panchami story?
faq.a: The best-known story comes from the Mahabharata. King Janamejaya, grieving his father Parikshit's death from Takshaka's bite, performed a sacrifice to destroy all snakes. The young sage Astika, himself half naga, came to the ritual and persuaded the king to stop. The snakes were spared, and tradition marks that mercy on Naga Panchami.

faq.q: Why are snakes worshipped in Hinduism?
faq.a: Snakes appear throughout Hindu stories: Shesha supports Vishnu, Vasuki coils around Shiva's neck, and nagas guard water and treasure beneath the earth. They are associated with fertility, the monsoon, time and renewal, because they shed their skin. Worship is usually offered to stone images of nagas or at anthills; live snakes are left alone.

posts.title: Krishna Janmashtami at Home: A Midnight for Beginners
posts.description: Krishna Janmashtami at home for beginners in the USA: tiny footprints, a cradle, butter and a midnight you can actually keep on a school night with kids.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Krishna was born at midnight in a prison. You do not need a temple to keep that hour; you need a small cradle, a bowl of butter and the willingness to be awake when the house is quiet.

## Krishna Janmashtami at home: what you need — a small cradle or basket, a picture or small image of baby Krishna, butter, aval, fruit, tulsi, a lamp; rice-flour footprints from the door to the puja corner, as Gokulashtami homes draw them

## Why midnight, and do you have to stay up? — the Bhagavata Purana's birth in Mathura at midnight in Rohini, on the eighth day of the waning moon; the vigil as attention, not endurance; an earlier 'midnight' for young children

## A beginner's evening, hour by hour — a light fast or simple meal, singing or reading the birth story, a short abhishekam, rocking the cradle at the birth hour, sharing butter and sweets; time-zone notes for watching Mathura or Udupi
Close: try this for a week after Janmashtami: before sleep, sit two minutes in the dark with one lamp. That is the whole midnight, practised small.
takeaways: To keep Krishna Janmashtami at home, draw small footprints to the puja corner, set up a cradle, fast lightly, and offer butter and aval at the midnight hour of his birth.
The midnight vigil is a practice of attention, not endurance; families with young children often mark the birth earlier in the evening.

faq.q: How do I do janmashtami puja at home simple?
faq.a: Clean the puja space and set up a small cradle with a picture or image of baby Krishna. Light a lamp and offer tulsi, flowers, butter, aval, milk sweets and fruit. Chant 'Om Namo Bhagavate Vasudevaya' or sing a bhajan, read the birth story, and at the chosen hour rock the cradle, do aarti, and share the offerings.

faq.q: Why are Krishna's footprints drawn for Gokulashtami?
faq.a: In many South Indian homes, gokulashtami Krishna footprints are drawn with rice flour paste from the front door to the puja room, small and baby-sized. They show little Krishna walking into the house to steal butter and bless the family. Children love making them by pressing the side of a closed fist into the paste and adding toes with a fingertip.

faq.q: What is the Janmashtami midnight puja time in the USA?
faq.a: The puja is timed to the midnight of the day when the eighth day of the waning moon, ashtami, is in force, ideally with Rohini star. Calculate it for your own location, not India's; a US panchangam or your local temple lists the nishita puja time. Families with small children often do the main puja earlier and a short prayer at midnight.

faq.q: When is Krishna Janmashtami celebrated?
faq.a: Janmashtami falls on the eighth day of the waning moon in Shravana or Bhadrapada, depending on the calendar your family follows, usually August or September. Smarta and Vaishnava communities sometimes observe it on consecutive days. Check the current year's panchangam for your region and your family's tradition.

posts.title: Ganesh Chaturthi in the USA: Clay, Community, Care
posts.description: Ganesh Chaturthi in the USA: bringing home a clay Ganesha, keeping it on a weekday, finding a community celebration, and immersion when lakes are off limits.
posts.author: manikandan
secondaryKeywords: where to buy clay ganesha in usa
ganesh chaturthi celebration at home usa
outline: Hook: The first Ganesha we brought home in New Jersey came from a folding table in a temple parking lot, wrapped in newspaper, and sat on my son's lap in the back seat all the way to Edison.

## How do families keep Ganesh Chaturthi in the USA? — the fourth day of the bright half of Bhadrapada, usually August or September; bringing home a clay Ganesha; one-and-a-half, three, five or ten days depending on family custom and work schedules

## The home puja, on a Tuesday if need be — pranapratishta by a priest or a simple invocation, twenty-one blades of durva grass, kozhukattai or modak, a lamp at morning and evening; not looking at the moon that night, and the Syamantaka jewel story behind it

## Community: temples, pandals and the immersion question — temple processions on the nearest weekend, community halls, the local rules that keep idols out of lakes, dissolving the clay in water at home and returning it to the garden
Close: Avvaiyar sang her Vinayagar Agaval to Ganesha; this week, keep him in mind at one doorway, the front door, every time you leave.
takeaways: In the USA, families bring home a clay Ganesha for Ganesh Chaturthi, keep a simple puja for one to ten days, and join temple celebrations on the nearest weekend.
Since most local waters are off limits for immersion, many dissolve the clay Ganesha at home in a bucket and pour the water into the garden.

faq.q: Where to buy clay Ganesha in the USA?
faq.a: Many Hindu temples in the US sell clay Ganesha images in the weeks before Chaturthi, and Indian grocery stores often stock them. Community groups hold workshops where families shape their own from natural clay. Look for unpainted or naturally coloured clay so it dissolves easily in water. Order or reserve early, because popular sizes sell out.

faq.q: How do I do a Ganesh Chaturthi celebration at home in the USA?
faq.a: Set up a clean platform with a cloth, place the clay Ganesha, and invoke him with a lamp, flowers, durva grass and a short prayer, or ask a priest to do pranapratishta. Offer modak or kozhukattai and fruit, do aarti morning and evening, and invite friends. After one and a half to ten days, do a farewell puja and immerse the image.

faq.q: Do US temples celebrate Ganesh Chaturthi?
faq.a: Yes. Ganesh Chaturthi at US temples usually brings abhishekam, special pujas, and often a multi-day festival, clay Ganesha workshops for children and a procession. Because the festival often falls on a weekday, the biggest community events usually take place on the nearest weekend. Check your local temple's schedule a few weeks ahead.

faq.q: Why shouldn't you look at the moon on Ganesh Chaturthi?
faq.a: The story says Ganesha, after a big meal of modak, tripped and his belly burst, and the moon laughed at him. Ganesha cursed that anyone seeing the moon on Chaturthi would face false accusation. Krishna himself, the Bhagavata Purana says, was falsely accused over the Syamantaka jewel. Hearing that story is the traditional remedy for an accidental glance.

posts.title: Eco-Friendly Ganesh Visarjan at Home, in a Bucket
posts.description: Eco friendly Ganesh visarjan at home: choosing natural clay, the farewell puja, dissolving Ganesha in a bucket, and giving the water back to the garden.
posts.author: archana
secondaryKeywords: ganesh visarjan at home in bucket
outline: Hook: Visarjan means letting go. You can do it in a bucket on your back porch and lose nothing of the meaning; you may even understand it better, because you watch the whole return.
## Eco friendly Ganesh visarjan starts at the store — unbaked natural clay (shadu), no plaster of Paris, no oil paint or glitter; seed Ganesha images; the smaller the image, the easier the goodbye

## How do you do visarjan at home in a bucket? — the uttara puja: a last aarti, akshata, modak and a sankalpam asking Ganesha to return; carrying him to a clean bucket of water, lowering him slowly, chanting 'Ganapati Bappa Morya'

## What to do with the water and the clay — letting it dissolve over a day or two, stirring gently, pouring the water into plants or a garden bed, keeping a pinch of clay for a pot; flowers go to compost
Close: try this: sit with the bucket for five minutes after immersion and watch the form soften. That is the practice: letting something you loved go back to where it came from.
takeaways: An eco friendly Ganesh visarjan uses unbaked natural clay, a farewell puja at home, and a bucket of water in which the image dissolves over a day or two.
The dissolved clay and water go back into a garden or potted plants, and flowers and leaves go to compost, completing the cycle the festival describes.

faq.q: How do you do Ganesh visarjan at home in a bucket?
faq.a: After the farewell puja, fill a clean bucket or tub with enough water to cover the image. Carry Ganesha to it with the family, say a short prayer asking him to return, and lower the image in gently. Leave it to dissolve, stirring now and then. Once the clay has settled, pour the water and clay into your garden or potted plants.

faq.q: How long does it take to dissolve clay Ganesha?
faq.a: An unbaked natural clay Ganesha usually softens within hours and dissolves fully in one to two days, depending on size and thickness. Stirring the water gently helps. Painted or baked images, and those made of plaster of Paris, may not dissolve at all, which is why natural clay is recommended. Remove any decorations before immersion.

faq.q: What are the Ganesh visarjan puja steps?
faq.a: The farewell, called uttara puja, begins with lighting the lamp and offering flowers, durva grass, akshata, modak and fruit. The family does a final aarti, asks forgiveness for any lapses, and moves the image slightly to signal departure. Then Ganesha is carried to the water with chanting and immersed. Some families tie a little curd rice in a cloth for his journey.

posts.title: Onam and Mahabali: The King Who Comes Home
posts.description: Onam significance: Mahabali, the generous king who asked to visit his people each year, and what the pookalam, the sadya and the homecoming really celebrate.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: Most stories about asuras end with a defeat. Onam's story ends with an asura king pushed into the underworld, and an entire people setting flowers at the door so he will feel welcome when he visits.

## Onam significance: a festival for the one who lost — Thiruvonam star in the Malayalam month of Chingam, usually August or September; the harvest season in Kerala; the memory of a reign when, the song says, all people were equal

## What happened between Mahabali and Vamana? — the Bhagavata Purana story of the dwarf who asked for three steps of land; the king who kept his word even when his guru warned him; the one boon he asked: to see his people once a year

## Pookalam, sadya and the ten days — flower carpets growing from Atham to Thiruvonam, the Onathappan clay figures, the sadya on a banana leaf, boat races and swings; the story is really about hospitality as the highest virtue
Close: a gentle reframe: Onam does not celebrate who won. It celebrates who is welcomed home. Set a place for someone who has been away.
takeaways: Onam is Kerala's harvest festival, culminating on Thiruvonam in Chingam, celebrating King Mahabali's annual return to see his people.
In the story, Vamana takes Mahabali's kingdom in three steps, but Mahabali's generosity earns him one boon: to come home once a year.

faq.q: Why is Onam celebrated?
faq.a: Onam is celebrated to welcome King Mahabali, who, in Kerala tradition, ruled a golden age of equality and plenty and visits his people once a year. It is also the harvest festival of Kerala. Families lay flower carpets called pookalam, wear new clothes, prepare the grand Onasadya feast, and enjoy boat races, games and dances across ten days.

faq.q: What is the Onam Mahabali story?
faq.a: Mahabali, a generous asura king, grew so powerful that the gods felt displaced. Vishnu came as Vamana, a young dwarf Brahmin, and asked for three steps of land. Mahabali agreed despite his guru's warning. Vamana grew immense, covered earth and sky in two steps, and Mahabali offered his own head for the third, asking only to visit his people yearly.

faq.q: What happens on the ten days of Onam?
faq.a: The ten days of Onam run from Atham star to Thiruvonam. Each day the pookalam at the doorstep grows by a new ring of flowers. Families shop and clean in the early days, prepare clay Onathappan figures, and gather on Uthradam and Thiruvonam for the sadya, a feast of many dishes served on a banana leaf.
