outline: Hook: The suitcase home from India always carries a small temple: ghee from my mother, kumkum from an aunt, a packet of prasadam, and each item travels differently.

## Carrying puja items on flight: the liquids and powders — ghee and oils treated like liquids or gels, kumkum, turmeric and vibhuti as powders that may get extra screening; pack in sealed tubs inside checked bags and check current TSA and airline guidance
## Can you carry coconut and camphor on a plane? — dry versus fresh coconut, why camphor is often refused as a flammable item, and buying camphor and lamps locally instead
## Customs, prasadam and declaring food — declare sweets, seeds and plant items when entering the USA, label them in English, keep laddus sealed; ask current customs guidance rather than old stories
Close: One small thing to carry — make a short list of what you can buy at the Indian store in Edison or wherever you live, and carry only what cannot be replaced
takeaways: When carrying puja items on a flight, pack ghee and oils in sealed tubs in checked bags, since carry-on liquid limits usually apply.
Camphor is often refused because it is flammable; many families buy camphor and lamps locally instead.
Declare prasadam, sweets and plant items at customs, and check current airline, security and customs guidance before you fly.

faq.q: Can I carry ghee in a flight?
faq.a: Ghee is usually treated like a liquid or gel, so carry-on limits apply. Most families pack it in a sealed plastic tub, wrapped twice, inside checked luggage. Airline and security rules change and differ by country, so check the current guidance for your route before packing. Warm climates soften ghee, so a leak-proof container matters more than anything.

faq.q: Can I carry a coconut on a plane?
faq.a: Dry, husked coconuts are often allowed in checked luggage, but rules on fresh coconuts, coconut water and plant material differ by country and airline. When entering the USA, declare it as a food item. Many families simply buy coconuts for pooja at a local Indian grocery, which avoids the question entirely. Check current guidance for your route.

faq.q: Can I bring prasadam from India to the USA?
faq.a: Many families bring sealed temple prasadam such as laddus, dry sweets and vibhuti. Declare all food items on your customs form and keep them in original packaging if possible. Items with meat, fresh fruit, seeds or soil may be refused. Customs rules change, so check current guidance. PariharaOnline can also ship prasadam from temples if carrying is difficult.

posts.title: Asking School for a Day Off for a Hindu Festival
posts.description: How to ask for a school holiday for Diwali or another Hindu festival: a short note to the teacher, religious absence policies, and helping your child explain.
posts.author: manikandan
secondaryKeywords: letter to teacher for diwali absence
outline: Hook: The first time I wrote to my son's teacher about Deepavali, I overthought it for a week; the reply came in ten minutes and asked if he could tell the class about lamps.
## Is Diwali an excused absence? — many districts excuse religious observance and a growing number close for Diwali; check your district's policy and the school calendar early

## School holiday for Diwali: writing the note — three sentences: the festival, the date, the request; offer to share a lamp or a sweet with the class; the same note works for Pongal, Navratri or Ganesh Chaturthi
## Helping your child explain the day — one line about light over darkness, a clay diya to show, the oil bath and new clothes in the morning; an eleven-year-old's version is often better than mine
Close: One small thing to carry — put the lunar festival dates for the school year in the family calendar the week school starts
takeaways: Many US school districts excuse absences for religious holidays, and some close for Diwali; check your district policy first.
A short, friendly note to the teacher naming the festival and the date is usually all that is needed.
Offering to share a lamp, a sweet or a short explanation turns an absence into a moment of inclusion.

faq.q: Is a religious holiday an excused absence in US schools?
faq.a: In many districts, yes. School policies often list religious observance as an excused absence, provided parents notify the school in advance. Some districts now close schools for Diwali. Policies differ by state and district, so read your school handbook or ask the office. Giving notice early also lets teachers plan around tests and assignments.

faq.q: How do I write a letter to a teacher for a Diwali absence?
faq.a: Keep it short and warm. Name the festival, give the date, say your child will be absent to celebrate with family, and ask for any work to catch up on. You might add one line explaining that Diwali is the festival of lights. Many parents also offer to send sweets or visit the class to talk about it.

faq.q: Which US schools have a holiday for Diwali?
faq.a: A growing number of districts, including some in New York, New Jersey and other states with large South Asian communities, now list Diwali on the school calendar. Many others do not but excuse the absence. Check your own district's calendar, and if the day is not listed, a respectful request to the school board is a common way families raise it.

posts.title: Your US-Born Baby's Birth Star: Time Zones Explained
posts.description: Finding the nakshatra for a baby born in the US: why the Moon's star is one worldwide at one instant, how time zones shift the date, what to tell an astrologer.
posts.author: hariharan
posts.primaryKeyword: nakshatra for a baby born in the us
secondaryKeywords: janma nakshatra for baby born abroad
outline: Hook: A baby born at night in Texas and one born at the same instant in Chennai share a birth star, because the Moon sits in the same place in the sky for both; only the clock and the calendar disagree.

## One sky, many clocks — the nakshatra as the Moon's position among twenty-seven stars, the old image of the Moon visiting a different star-wife each night; why the position is universal and the local date is not

## How is the nakshatra for baby born in USA worked out? — exact birth time, city and time zone, daylight saving; converting to IST only to compare with an Indian panchangam; when the star changes near the birth hour

## What changes with place, and what does not — the lagna (rising sign) and houses depend on the birth city, the nakshatra does not; the star birthday each year may fall a day apart in India and America
Close: The reframe — the child belongs to one sky; give the astrologer the local time and place and let the numbers do the rest
takeaways: The nakshatra for a baby born in the USA depends on the Moon's position at the birth instant, which is the same everywhere in the world.
What changes with place is the local date, the rising sign and the houses, so give the astrologer exact local time and city.
When the Moon changes stars near the birth hour, careful time-zone conversion matters, including daylight saving.

faq.q: Does birth place change the nakshatra?
faq.a: Not directly. The nakshatra is the star the Moon occupies at the moment of birth, and at any single instant the Moon is in the same place for everyone on Earth. Birth place changes the local date, the rising sign and the houses of the chart. If the Moon changed stars near the birth time, accurate conversion becomes important.

faq.q: How is the birth star calculated across time zones?
faq.a: The astrologer converts the local birth time, including daylight saving, into a single reference time, often Universal Time or Indian Standard Time, then finds where the Moon was at that instant. That position gives the nakshatra and its pada, the quarter used for naming syllables. Accurate minutes matter most when the Moon was close to moving into the next star.

faq.q: What details should I give an astrologer for a baby born abroad?
faq.a: Give the exact birth time from the hospital record, the date, the city and state, and mention whether daylight saving was in effect. Do not convert the time yourself; let the astrologer do it. Having the parents' stars and family traditions for naming helps too. A good astrologer will explain which details affect the janma nakshatra.

posts.title: What Is Moksha? Freedom, Not an Exit
posts.description: What is moksha? Not an escape from life but freedom within it. Nachiketa's questions to Yama in the Katha Upanishad, and what liberation really means.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: Moksha is usually translated as liberation and pictured as an exit from the world; the Katha Upanishad tells it through a boy who walks into the house of Death and asks the one question Death would rather not answer.

## What is moksha, in plain words? — freedom from samsara, the cycle of birth and death, and more deeply from the sense of a small, separate self; the fourth of the four aims of life, after dharma, artha and kama

## Nachiketa at Yama's door — the three boons; Yama's offers of wealth, long life and pleasure, all refused; the teaching on the self that is not born and does not die; the story is really about choosing the lasting (shreyas) over the merely pleasant (preyas)

## Can you be free while still living? — jivanmukti, liberation while embodied, in Advaita and in lives like Ramana Maharshi's; how Advaita, Vishishtadvaita, Dvaita and the bhakti traditions describe moksha differently
Close: A gentle reframe — moksha may be less a door out of the world than a way of standing in it without being gripped
takeaways: Moksha means liberation: freedom from the cycle of rebirth and, more deeply, from identifying with a small, anxious, separate self.
Hindu schools describe moksha differently, as oneness with Brahman or as loving nearness to God, but all see it as life's highest aim.

faq.q: What is the meaning of moksha in Hinduism?
faq.a: Moksha means release or liberation. In Hindu thought it is the last of the four aims of life and refers to freedom from samsara, the cycle of birth and death driven by karma. Philosophically, it means seeing through the limited sense of self. Advaita calls it realising oneness with Brahman; devotional schools describe it as eternal closeness to God.

faq.q: What is the difference between moksha and nirvana?
faq.a: Both words point to liberation, but they come from different frameworks. Moksha is the Hindu term, usually described as realising the true self, the atman, or as union or closeness with the divine. Nirvana is central to Buddhism, where it means the blowing out of craving and of the illusion of a lasting self. The overlap is real; the explanations differ.

faq.q: Can someone attain moksha while still alive?
faq.a: Many Hindu teachers say yes. The idea is called jivanmukti, liberation while living. A jivanmukta continues to eat, speak and act, but is no longer driven by fear, craving or a sense of separateness. Advaita Vedanta in particular teaches this, and devotees often point to saints such as Ramana Maharshi as examples. Other schools place final liberation after death.

posts.title: Atman and Brahman: Who Is Asking 'Who Am I?'
posts.description: Atman and Brahman, tried rather than debated: the Chandogya Upanishad's salt in water, Tat tvam asi, and a simple 'Who am I?' practice for one week.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Atman is the self you actually are, Brahman is the reality everything is made of, and the Upanishads' boldest claim is that they are the same; you cannot settle that by argument, but you can look at who is asking.
## Atman and Brahman in one breath — atman, the innermost self behind body and thought; Brahman, the ground of all that exists; the Mandukya Upanishad's 'Ayam atma brahma', this self is Brahman

## Salt in water: Uddalaka's lesson to Shvetaketu — in the Chandogya Upanishad a father dissolves salt in water and has his son taste it from every side, invisible yet everywhere; Tat tvam asi, you are that

## Who is asking 'Who am I?' — a practice: sit for ten minutes, notice a thought, a sensation, a mood, and ask who notices; the self-inquiry associated with Ramana Maharshi, offered as experience rather than doctrine
Close: Try this for a week — once a day, when you feel irritated, ask quietly, 'Who is irritated?' and watch what happens to the irritation
takeaways: Atman is your innermost self and Brahman is the reality underlying everything; the Upanishads teach that the two are ultimately one.
The Chandogya Upanishad's salt-in-water lesson and the phrase Tat tvam asi, you are that, present this unity as something to be seen, not merely believed.

faq.q: What is the difference between atman and Brahman?
faq.a: Atman refers to the self as experienced from within: the awareness behind your body, thoughts and emotions. Brahman refers to the ultimate reality behind the entire universe. In Advaita Vedanta the difference is only one of viewpoint, since atman is Brahman. Other Hindu schools see the individual self as a real part of Brahman, or as eternally distinct yet dependent.

faq.q: What does tat tvam asi mean?
faq.a: Tat tvam asi is Sanskrit for you are that. It comes from the Chandogya Upanishad, where the sage Uddalaka repeats it to his son Shvetaketu while teaching him through examples such as salt dissolved in water. It is counted among the great sayings, the mahavakyas, of Vedanta and points to the identity of the individual self with Brahman.

faq.q: How do I practise 'Who am I?' self inquiry at home?
faq.a: Sit comfortably for ten minutes. Let thoughts, sounds and sensations come. Each time you notice one, ask quietly, who is aware of this? Do not answer with words; simply turn attention back toward the one who notices. Many people find the mind grows quieter. This method is associated with Ramana Maharshi, who taught it as a direct path.

posts.title: Maya Meaning: Not Illusion, Exactly
posts.description: Maya meaning in Hinduism, told through Narada asking Vishnu to show him maya and being sent for a glass of water. Why maya is less 'illusion' than forgetting.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: Narada once asked Vishnu to show him maya, and Vishnu asked him to fetch a glass of water first; by the time Narada came back, a whole lifetime had passed.

## The story of Narada and the glass of water — a Puranic story told in many versions: Narada reaches a village, marries, raises children, loses everything in a flood, and wakes to find Vishnu still waiting for his water

## Maya meaning in Hinduism: not 'unreal', but misread — the word often linked to a root meaning to measure; maya as the power by which the one appears as many; in chapter 7 of the Gita, Krishna calls it his divine maya, hard to cross

## Is the world an illusion, then? — Advaita calls the world mithya, neither simply real nor simply unreal; bhakti traditions see maya as the Goddess or as lila, divine play; the story is really about getting so absorbed in the play that you forget who is playing
Close: A gentle reframe — maya is not the world, it is the forgetting; the glass of water is still in your hand
takeaways: In Hinduism, maya is the power that makes one reality appear as many separate things, and the forgetting that follows; it does not simply mean the world is fake.
The story of Narada and the glass of water shows maya as absorption: a whole life lived so fully that the seeker forgets what he came for.

faq.q: What is maya in Vedanta?
faq.a: In Vedanta, maya is the power through which the one reality, Brahman, appears as a world of many separate names and forms. Advaita Vedanta describes the world as mithya, neither wholly real nor wholly unreal, like a dream while you are inside it. Devotional schools treat maya as the Lord's own power, which both hides and reveals him.

faq.q: What is the story of Narada and Vishnu's maya?
faq.a: In a popular Puranic story, the sage Narada asks Vishnu to explain maya. Vishnu asks him to fetch water first. At a village, Narada falls in love, marries and raises a family, until a flood sweeps everything away. Weeping, he hears Vishnu ask, where is my water? Only moments have passed. The story shows how completely we lose ourselves in experience.

faq.q: Does maya mean the world is not real?
faq.a: Not exactly. Most Hindu teachers say the world is real as experience, but not ultimately what it seems. The problem is not the world but misunderstanding it, taking the changing for the permanent and the separate self for the whole truth. Bhakti traditions go further and call the world lila, divine play, to be enjoyed without clinging.

posts.title: Reincarnation in Hinduism: What the Texts Actually Say
posts.description: Reincarnation in Hinduism, from the texts: the Gita's worn-out clothes, the Upanishads' caterpillar on a blade of grass, and what is said to be reborn.
posts.author: hariharan
secondaryKeywords: what the bhagavad gita says about rebirth
outline: Hook: The Bhagavad Gita compares rebirth to changing clothes: the self sets aside worn garments and puts on new ones; the image comforts, but the texts say more, and they do not all say the same thing.

## What do the texts actually say about reincarnation in Hinduism? — punarjanma (rebirth) and samsara (the round of wandering); the clothing image in chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga; the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's caterpillar that reaches for the next blade of grass before letting go of the last
## What is it that is reborn? — the atman itself does not change; the subtle body carrying impressions (samskaras) moves on; the Katha Upanishad and the Gita on the self as unborn and undying

## Is rebirth a punishment? — schools and teachers differ on the details; rebirth read as continuity of learning rather than a sentence; moksha as release from the round rather than escape from a courtroom
Close: A gentle reframe — whether or not you hold to rebirth, the texts ask the same question of this life: which tendencies are you strengthening today?
takeaways: Hinduism teaches punarjanma, rebirth: the unchanging self, the atman, passes through many lives, carried by a subtle body shaped by past actions and tendencies.
The Bhagavad Gita compares rebirth to setting aside worn clothes for new ones; the aim is moksha, release from the cycle altogether.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about rebirth?
faq.a: In chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, Krishna tells Arjuna that the self is never born and never dies. Just as a person discards worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the embodied self leaves an old body and takes a new one. The teaching is meant to steady Arjuna's grief, not to frighten him, by pointing to what does not perish.

faq.q: What is the meaning of punarjanma?
faq.a: Punarjanma is the Sanskrit word for rebirth, literally being born again. It describes the belief that the self continues after death and takes on a new body, carrying the impressions of earlier lives. Punarjanma belongs to the larger idea of samsara, the round of births and deaths, which Hindu philosophy hopes to transcend through knowledge, devotion and selfless action.

faq.q: Do all Hindus believe in reincarnation?
faq.a: Most Hindu traditions accept rebirth, and it is assumed in the Upanishads, the Gita and the Puranas. But Hinduism has no single creed, and people hold it in different ways: some literally, some as a symbol of continuity, some with open questions. Many practising Hindus focus less on past lives and more on living this one with care.

posts.title: The Four Purusharthas: Wealth and Pleasure Are Allowed
posts.description: The four purusharthas, dharma, artha, kama and moksha, say wealth and pleasure are legitimate aims of life. A Sunday column on balancing all four.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: Hinduism names four aims of a good life, and two of them are wealth and pleasure; I learned that not in a scripture class but from my Thatha, who said a cloth merchant who does not want profit should become a monk instead.

## What are the four purusharthas? — dharma (right conduct), artha (wealth and security), kama (pleasure, love, beauty) and moksha (liberation); how the Tirukkural's three books, Aram, Porul and Inbam, map onto the first three
## Why wealth and pleasure are allowed — artha and kama are aims to pursue within dharma, not temptations to defeat; the salary, the holiday, the good meal; guilt as a misreading of the tradition
## How do the four purusharthas fit a working week? — dharma as the frame, artha and kama as the contents, moksha as the direction; a commute, a promotion, a family dinner, a quiet minute at the lamp
Close: One small thing for the week — at the end of each day, ask which of the four you served, and whether dharma held the others in place
takeaways: The four purusharthas are dharma, artha, kama and moksha: right conduct, wealth, pleasure and liberation, the four aims of a full human life.
Hindu tradition treats wealth and pleasure as legitimate when pursued within dharma; renunciation is one path, not a requirement.

faq.q: What do dharma, artha, kama and moksha mean?
faq.a: They are the four purusharthas, the aims of human life. Dharma is right conduct and duty. Artha is wealth, work and material security. Kama is pleasure, love, art and enjoyment. Moksha is liberation from the cycle of rebirth and from a narrow sense of self. Together they describe a life that is engaged with the world and also pointed beyond it.

faq.q: Is it wrong for a Hindu to want money?
faq.a: No. Artha, wealth and material well-being, is one of the four recognised aims of life. Texts from the Mahabharata to the Tirukkural treat honest earning as a duty, especially for householders who support families and give to others. The caution is about means and balance: wealth pursued against dharma, or at the cost of every other aim, is what the tradition warns against.

faq.q: Which purushartha is most important?
faq.a: Traditionally, moksha is called the highest aim, and dharma is the one that governs the other three. But most teachers do not rank them as a ladder to be climbed by abandoning the lower rungs. For a householder, a balanced life gives each its place: dharma as the frame, artha and kama as its content, and moksha as the direction.

posts.title: Three Gunas Explained: Sattva, Rajas, Tamas in Your Day
posts.description: The three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, observed in one ordinary day: the foggy morning, the afternoon rush, the calm evening, and what tips the balance.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: You can see the three gunas in a single day: the heaviness before coffee, the rush after lunch, the clear hour when the house goes quiet; the tradition named them so you could learn to notice them.

## What are the three gunas? — from Sankhya philosophy and chapter 14 of the Bhagavad Gita, Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga: sattva (clarity, balance), rajas (activity, restlessness), tamas (inertia, heaviness); every mind and body is a mix

## The three gunas in your day — morning tamas, workday rajas, pockets of sattva; how sleep, screens, food and company tilt the balance; chapter 17 on food and the gunas as a traditional lens, not a diet plan

## Is tamas bad and sattva good? — each has a role: tamas lets you sleep, rajas gets things built, sattva lets you see; the Gita's ideal is to go beyond all three (gunatita), not to cling even to sattva
Close: Try this for a week — three times a day, pause and name which guna is running the show, without trying to change it
takeaways: The three gunas are sattva, rajas and tamas: clarity, activity and inertia, the qualities that the Bhagavad Gita says colour every mind, meal and action.
No guna is simply bad; sleep needs tamas and work needs rajas, but noticing which one dominates is the first step to shifting it.

faq.q: What do sattva, rajas and tamas mean?
faq.a: They are the three gunas, or qualities of nature. Sattva is clarity, lightness and harmony. Rajas is energy, passion and restlessness. Tamas is heaviness, inertia and dullness. Sankhya philosophy and the Bhagavad Gita teach that everything in nature, including your moods and habits, is some mixture of these three, constantly shifting in balance.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about the gunas?
faq.a: The Gita discusses the gunas in several places, most fully in chapter 14, Gunatraya Vibhaga Yoga. Krishna explains how sattva binds through attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas through attachment to action, and tamas through negligence and sleep. Chapter 17 applies the gunas to faith, food and giving. The ideal is to rise beyond all three.

faq.q: What are sattvic, rajasic and tamasic foods?
faq.a: In traditional teaching, sattvic foods are fresh, light and nourishing, such as fruit, vegetables, grains, milk and ghee. Rajasic foods are very spicy, salty or stimulating. Tamasic foods are stale, reheated many times or heavy enough to leave you sluggish. Treat these as a lens for noticing how food affects you, not as strict rules or medical advice.

posts.title: Advaita Explained Simply, With a Pot and Some Space
posts.description: Advaita Vedanta explained simply with a clay pot and the space inside it: when the pot breaks, the space goes nowhere. Plus Shankara's rope and snake.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: Take a clay pot; the space inside seems to belong to the pot, but when the pot breaks the space goes nowhere, because it was never separate; that is most of Advaita in one image.

## Advaita Vedanta explained simply: not-two — Advaita means non-dual; Brahman alone is real and the self, atman, is not other than Brahman; Adi Shankara's commentaries on the Upanishads, the Gita and the Brahma Sutras
## The pot and the space — pot-space (ghatakasha) and great space (mahakasha), a classic Advaita image; the story is really about limits that feel real without being final

## Then why do I feel separate? — the rope in dim light mistaken for a snake: the fear is real, the snake is not; ignorance (avidya) and knowledge (jnana); how Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita keep the devotee and God distinct
Close: A gentle reframe — Advaita does not ask you to stop seeing pots; it asks you to remember the space
takeaways: Advaita Vedanta teaches that reality is non-dual: the individual self, atman, is not separate from Brahman, the one reality behind everything.
Its classic images are space inside a pot, unchanged when the pot breaks, and a rope mistaken for a snake: the error lies in perception, not in reality.

faq.q: What is Advaita in simple words?
faq.a: Advaita means not two. It is a school of Vedanta, systematised by Adi Shankara, which teaches that there is only one reality, Brahman, and that your deepest self is identical with it. The sense of being a separate, limited person is compared to space appearing divided by the walls of a pot. Liberation is seeing this clearly.

faq.q: What is the rope and snake analogy in Advaita?
faq.a: In dim light, a person sees a coiled rope and mistakes it for a snake. Their fear is real and their heart races, yet there was only ever a rope. When a lamp is brought, the snake disappears, but nothing is destroyed. Advaita uses this to explain how the world of separation is superimposed on Brahman, and how knowledge removes the error.

faq.q: How is Advaita different from Dvaita?
faq.a: Advaita, taught by Adi Shankara, says the individual self and Brahman are ultimately one. Dvaita, taught by Madhvacharya, says they are eternally distinct: the soul depends on God but never merges with him. Vishishtadvaita, taught by Ramanuja, sits between them, seeing souls as real parts of God. All three are Vedanta, reading the same core texts differently.

posts.title: Ahimsa in Daily Life: Harm Less, Starting Small
posts.description: Ahimsa meaning, beyond vegetarianism: non-harm in words, at work, at home and at the dinner table, with one small practice to begin this week.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: Ahimsa means non-harm, and it begins long before the dinner plate; I saw it one evening when my son carried a spider out of the bathroom in a paper cup rather than let me reach for a shoe.

## Ahimsa meaning: more than not hitting — a-himsa, the absence of the wish to harm; the first yama in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, the Mahabharata's 'ahimsa paramo dharmah', and the Tirukkural's chapter Innaa Seyyaamai (Not Doing Harm)
## Where does harm hide in an ordinary day? — the sharp email, the joke at a colleague's expense, the impatient horn, the careless purchase; ahimsa as a filter on words and choices, not only on food
## Is ahimsa the same as being a pushover? — Gandhi's non-violent resistance; the Gita's battlefield and the difference between harm and duty; protecting others without hatred
Close: One small thing for the week — pick one habitual harm, in speech, in food or in hurry, and soften it for seven days
takeaways: Ahimsa means non-harm: the absence of intent to injure any living being in action, word or thought, and it is the first ethical restraint in yoga.
Practising ahimsa starts small, with gentler words, less careless consumption and fewer reactions in anger, long before it becomes a question of diet.

faq.q: What is the meaning of ahimsa paramo dharma?
faq.a: Ahimsa paramo dharmah is a Sanskrit phrase found in the Mahabharata, usually translated as non-violence is the highest duty. It became widely known through Gandhi, who made ahimsa the centre of his public life. The epic also discusses duty and the protection of others, so many teachers read it as non-harm as the highest ideal, balanced by responsibility.

faq.q: How can I practise ahimsa in daily life?
faq.a: Start with speech, since most daily harm happens there. Pause before a sharp reply, avoid gossip and mockery, and correct others privately. Then look at habits: driving, shopping, food and how you treat people who serve you. Choose one area and soften it for a week. Ahimsa grows through attention to small, repeated choices rather than dramatic vows.

faq.q: Does ahimsa mean Hindus must be vegetarian?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Many Hindus choose vegetarianism as an expression of ahimsa, and some traditions strongly encourage it, but practice varies widely by region, community and family. Ahimsa is broader than diet: it covers words, thoughts and actions toward every being. A person can reflect on ahimsa honestly whether or not they are vegetarian, and many move toward it gradually.

posts.title: Bhagavad Gita for Beginners: Where to Actually Start
posts.description: Bhagavad Gita for beginners: start with chapter 2, read slowly, keep a translation you trust, and let a single verse sit for a week. A practical way in.
posts.author: manikandan
secondaryKeywords: how to read the bhagavad gita
best bhagavad gita translation for beginners
which gita chapter to read first
outline: Hook: The best place to start the Bhagavad Gita is not verse one but chapter 2, where Krishna begins to answer; I learned that after three failed attempts to read it cover to cover on the train.

## What is the Gita, in a paragraph? — 700 verses in 18 chapters inside the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata; a conversation between Arjuna and Krishna on the field of Kurukshetra; why householders read it, not only monks

## Bhagavad Gita for beginners: a reading order — chapter 2 (Sankhya Yoga), then chapter 12 (Bhakti Yoga), then chapters 3 and 6; go back to chapter 1 once you care about Arjuna; one verse a day rather than one chapter

## Which translation should I read? — one with the Sanskrit, a word-by-word gloss and a plain rendering; a second one later to see the range; a commentary from one tradition gives depth, two give perspective
Close: One small thing for the week — choose a single verse, such as 2.47 on action without clinging to results, and read it every morning for seven days
takeaways: Beginners do best starting the Bhagavad Gita at chapter 2, where Krishna's teaching begins, then chapter 12 on devotion, reading a verse a day.
The Gita has 700 verses in 18 chapters; a translation with the Sanskrit, word meanings and plain English makes a steady companion.

faq.q: How should I start reading the Bhagavad Gita?
faq.a: Begin small and slow. Many readers start with chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, where Krishna begins his teaching, rather than chapter 1, which sets the scene. Read one or two verses each day, with a translation that shows the Sanskrit and word meanings. Keep a notebook for lines that stay with you. Finishing matters less than understanding.

faq.q: Which is the best Bhagavad Gita translation for beginners?
faq.a: The best translation is one you will actually read. Look for an edition that gives the Sanskrit verse, a transliteration, word-by-word meanings and a clear English rendering. Translations from different traditions, such as Advaita or Vaishnava lineages, emphasise different ideas, so read one first and a second later for contrast. Avoid starting with a very long commentary.

faq.q: Do I need to be religious to read the Gita?
faq.a: No. Many people read the Bhagavad Gita for its thinking on duty, action, fear and the mind, whether or not they worship Krishna. Its questions are universal: what to do when every option hurts, how to work without anxiety, how to stay steady. Devotional readers find more in it over time, but the door is open to anyone curious.

posts.title: Nishkama Karma: The Gita on Work Without Clinging
posts.description: Nishkama karma, the Gita's idea of work without clinging to results: what verse 2.47 says, why it is not indifference, and a week-long work practice.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Nishkama karma means doing the work fully and letting go of your grip on the result; try it on one task this week and notice where your attention goes when you stop checking the scoreboard.

## What is nishkama karma? — nishkama (without craving) and karma (action); Bhagavad Gita 2.47: your right is to the action, never to its fruits, and do not be attached to inaction either; chapter 3, Karma Yoga, on action as offering
## Why letting go of results improves the work — attention split between task and outcome; anxiety as attention leaking into the future; the craftsman's absorption versus refreshing the inbox
## Doesn't that mean not caring? — nishkama is not indifference: plan, aim, care about quality, then release the grip; the Gita's warning against inaction as much as against attachment
Close: Try this for a week — before one task each day, say 'this is my offering', work for twenty-five minutes without checking any outcome, then notice how it felt
takeaways: Nishkama karma is the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on action without craving for results: do your work completely, and release your grip on how it turns out.
It is not indifference; Gita 2.47 also warns against inaction, so you still plan and care, but you stop letting outcomes run your attention.

faq.q: What is the meaning of Bhagavad Gita 2.47?
faq.a: In verse 2.47, Krishna tells Arjuna that his right is to action alone, never to its fruits. He should not act for the sake of results, nor become attached to not acting. It is the core statement of nishkama karma: engage fully, do your duty well, and loosen your attachment to outcomes you cannot fully control.

faq.q: What is the meaning of karma yoga?
faq.a: Karma yoga is the path of selfless action, taught mainly in chapters 2 and 3 of the Bhagavad Gita. It means doing your duties with care while offering the results to something larger than yourself, whether you call it God, dharma or the common good. Work becomes a practice for loosening ego and anxiety, rather than only a means of self-promotion.

faq.q: How do I practise detachment from results at work without losing motivation?
faq.a: Separate effort from outcome. Set clear goals, then spend your working time on the part you control: preparation, quality and attention. Check results at fixed times rather than constantly. When the outcome arrives, review it honestly and adjust. Many people find motivation actually improves, because energy once spent on worrying goes back into the work itself.

posts.title: Bhagavad Gita on Anxiety: What Krishna Told Arjuna
posts.description: Bhagavad Gita on anxiety: Arjuna's trembling limbs, Krishna's answer, and three practices from the Gita for an anxious mind, with room for real care.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: The Bhagavad Gita opens with something close to a panic attack: Arjuna's limbs give way, his mouth dries, his bow slips; what Krishna offers next is less a pep talk than a set of practices.

## Bhagavad Gita on anxiety: what happens to Arjuna — the list of bodily symptoms in chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, and his collapse onto the chariot seat; the text takes the body seriously before it offers philosophy

## What did Krishna tell Arjuna to do? — steadiness in pleasure and pain in chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga; action without clinging to outcome in verse 2.47; in chapter 6, Dhyana Yoga, the restless mind held through practice and detachment

## Three practices to try — anchor in body and breath with chapter 6's upright seat and steady gaze; act only on the next step; offer the outcome; all as support alongside professional help when anxiety is heavy
Close: Try this for a week — each morning, sit for five minutes as chapter 6 describes, spine upright, then name one action for the day and let its result go
takeaways: The Bhagavad Gita begins with Arjuna's body in panic, then offers practices: steady the mind through repeated practice, act on what you can do, and release the result.
The Gita can support an anxious mind, but it is not a substitute for medical or psychological care when anxiety is persistent or severe.

faq.q: Which Gita verses help with stress?
faq.a: Many readers return to three passages. Verse 2.47 teaches acting without clinging to results. The closing verses of chapter 2 describe the steady-minded person who is not shaken by pleasure or pain. Chapter 6, Dhyana Yoga, says the restless mind can be steadied through practice and detachment. Read one slowly each morning and see which settles you.

faq.q: What are Krishna's teachings on fear?
faq.a: Krishna does not tell Arjuna that fear is shameful. He first acknowledges the grief, then points Arjuna to what does not perish, the self, and to the duty in front of him. Fear loosens when attention returns from imagined futures to present action. Throughout the Gita, Krishna also offers refuge: surrendering the burden rather than carrying it alone.

faq.q: Can the Bhagavad Gita replace therapy for anxiety?
faq.a: No. The Gita offers a way of looking at action, fear and the mind that many people find steadying, and its practices of breath, attention and letting go can support wellbeing. But persistent or severe anxiety deserves proper care from a doctor or counsellor. Many people find the two work well together: professional help for the condition, the Gita for perspective.

posts.title: Arjuna's Despair: Why the Gita Begins With a Breakdown
posts.description: Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the Gita's first chapter, ends with a great warrior setting down his bow in despair. Why the teaching begins with a breakdown.
posts.author: hariharan
outline: Hook: The Gita does not begin with wisdom; it begins with a man falling apart, and the chapter in which Arjuna drops his bow is still called a yoga.

## The scene on the chariot — Dhritarashtra's question to Sanjaya, the conches blown (Krishna's Panchajanya, Arjuna's Devadatta), Arjuna asking Krishna to drive between the armies, seeing teachers and cousins, the bow Gandiva slipping from his hand
## Why is Arjuna Vishada Yoga called a yoga? — vishada means despair; the story is really about how a question has to be felt before an answer can land; despair as the doorway, not the obstacle

## What Arjuna's arguments reveal — reasons that sound noble (family, tradition, sin) and fear dressed as virtue; Krishna does not really begin until Arjuna says, early in chapter 2, that he is Krishna's student
Close: A gentle reframe — if you are stuck in your own first chapter, the Gita suggests you are exactly where the teaching starts
takeaways: Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the first chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, shows Arjuna collapsing in grief and refusing to fight; vishada means despair.
It is called a yoga because honest despair opens the door to learning; Krishna's teaching begins only once Arjuna admits he does not know what to do.

faq.q: What is a short summary of Bhagavad Gita chapter 1?
faq.a: Chapter 1, Arjuna Vishada Yoga, sets the scene on the battlefield of Kurukshetra. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks his charioteer Sanjaya what is happening. The armies blow their conches, and Arjuna asks Krishna to place their chariot between them. Seeing relatives and teachers on both sides, Arjuna is overwhelmed with grief, sets down his bow and sits in despair.

faq.q: Why did Arjuna refuse to fight?
faq.a: Arjuna saw his grandfather Bhishma, his teacher Drona, cousins and friends in the opposing army. He argued that killing kin would destroy families, traditions and his own peace, and that no kingdom was worth it. His reasons were partly compassion and partly fear and confusion. Krishna's teaching across the rest of the Gita responds to that tangle.

faq.q: Why is a chapter about despair called yoga?
faq.a: Every chapter of the Gita is named as a yoga, a discipline or way of joining. Calling Arjuna's despair a yoga suggests that the breakdown itself has value. Only when Arjuna admits he cannot solve his dilemma alone does he become ready to listen. Many readers find comfort in that: confusion can be the beginning of clarity.

posts.title: Sthitaprajna: The Gita's Picture of a Steady Mind
posts.description: Sthitaprajna meaning: the Gita's portrait of a person of steady wisdom, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs or an ocean that rivers cannot overfill.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Near the end of chapter 2, Arjuna asks a practical question: how does a person of steady wisdom speak, sit and walk; Krishna's answer is a portrait you can try on, one habit at a time.
## Sthitaprajna meaning — sthita (steady, established) and prajna (wisdom, insight); the closing verses of chapter 2, Sankhya Yoga, answering Arjuna's question about how such a person behaves

## The tortoise and the ocean — the tortoise drawing in its limbs as the senses withdraw from their objects; the ocean that stays full and still though rivers pour in, as desires enter without disturbing; free of craving, fear and anger

## Can an ordinary person become steady? — steadiness as a trained capacity, not a personality type; the chain in the same chapter from dwelling on objects to attachment, desire, anger and confusion; interrupting it early
Close: Try this for a week — once a day, when something pulls at you (a notification, a craving, a comment), withdraw your attention for ten breaths like the tortoise, then decide
takeaways: A sthitaprajna, in the Bhagavad Gita, is a person of steady wisdom: undisturbed by pleasure or pain, and free of craving, fear and anger.
Krishna pictures this steadiness as a tortoise drawing in its limbs and an ocean that stays still as rivers flow in; both describe trainable habits of attention.

faq.q: What are the sthitaprajna lakshana in the Gita?
faq.a: Lakshana means marks or signs. In the closing verses of chapter 2, Krishna lists the signs of a sthitaprajna: content in the self, unshaken by sorrow, not craving pleasure, free of attachment, fear and anger, and able to withdraw the senses at will, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs. Such a person finds peace without being driven by desire.

faq.q: What does steady wisdom mean in the Bhagavad Gita?
faq.a: Steady wisdom is a translation of sthitaprajna. It describes understanding that has become stable enough to hold under pressure, rather than insight that comes and goes. A person of steady wisdom still feels and acts, but events do not throw them off balance. The Gita presents this as the fruit of practice, detachment and self-knowledge, not as a gift for a few.

faq.q: How can I practise equanimity from the Gita?
faq.a: Start with a small pause. When something pulls your attention, a craving, a sharp comment, a worrying message, withdraw for ten breaths before responding, the way the Gita's tortoise draws in its limbs. Notice the urge rise and fall. Over weeks the gap widens. Equanimity is not suppressing feeling; it is feeling fully while choosing your response.

posts.title: Gita Chapter 12: The Short Chapter on Devotion
posts.description: Bhagavad Gita chapter 12, Bhakti Yoga, is only twenty verses: a ladder of devotion for every temperament and a portrait of the devotee Krishna holds dear.
posts.author: manikandan
outline: Hook: Chapter 12 of the Bhagavad Gita is the one I read in the hospital waiting room during my father's heart surgery, because it was short enough to finish and kind enough to stay with.

## What is Bhagavad Gita chapter 12 about? — Bhakti Yoga, the yoga of devotion, in twenty verses; Arjuna asks whether worship of God with form or meditation on the formless is better; Krishna honours both and calls devotion to the personal the easier road
## The ladder: if you cannot, then — fix the mind on Me; if not, practise; if not, work for My sake; if not, give up the fruits of action; a teaching that meets people where they are

## The devotee who is dear to Krishna — the closing verses: without hatred, friendly and compassionate, free of possessiveness, the same in honour and dishonour, content with whatever comes; qualities, not rituals
Close: One small thing for the week — pick one quality from the closing verses and practise it on the most difficult person you meet
takeaways: Bhagavad Gita chapter 12, Bhakti Yoga, is a short chapter of twenty verses on devotion, and a gentle place for beginners to start.
It offers a ladder for every temperament, from fixing the mind on God to simply giving up the fruits of action, and ends with the qualities of a beloved devotee.

faq.q: What is the summary of Gita chapter 12?
faq.a: In chapter 12, Bhakti Yoga, Arjuna asks whether devotion to God with form or meditation on the formless is better. Krishna says both reach him, but devotion to the personal God is easier for embodied beings. He then gives a graded path, from constant remembrance to renouncing the fruits of action, and closes by describing the qualities of devotees dear to him.

faq.q: What are the qualities of a devotee in the Gita?
faq.a: In the closing verses of chapter 12, Krishna describes a devotee dear to him as free of hatred, friendly and compassionate to all, without possessiveness or ego, patient, content and the same in pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour. Such a person neither agitates others nor is agitated by them. The list is about character rather than ritual, which is why it speaks so widely.

faq.q: Why do people recommend chapter 12 for daily reading?
faq.a: It is short, only twenty verses, and it is warm. Instead of demanding one practice, Krishna offers a series of options, so a reader can begin wherever they are. Many families recite it at home or read it during difficult times such as illness. Its final verses give a clear, practical list of qualities that can be worked on each day.

posts.title: How to Use a Japa Mala: 108 Beads, One Breath
posts.description: How to use a japa mala, step by step: holding the beads, the guru bead you never cross, which fingers to use, and pairing each bead with one slow breath.
posts.author: archana
posts.primaryKeyword: how to use a japa mala
secondaryKeywords: which finger to use for mala
outline: Hook: A japa mala is 108 beads and one larger bead, and learning how to use a japa mala takes about two minutes; try one round tomorrow morning, one bead per breath, and see how different it feels from counting in your head.
## How to use a japa mala, bead by bead — hold it in the right hand, draped over the middle or ring finger; move each bead toward you with the thumb; start beside the guru bead, the larger meru bead
## Why not cross the guru bead? — at the end of a round you turn the mala and go back; a tradition of respect for the teacher, and a physical cue that one round has ended

## Which beads, which finger, which mantra? — rudraksha for Shiva mantras, tulsi for Vishnu and Krishna, sandalwood or crystal as some traditions prefer; the index finger traditionally kept away; regional variations are fine
Close: Try this for a week: one round each morning, same seat, same mantra; let the fingers keep count so the mind can listen
takeaways: To use a japa mala, hold it in the right hand, move one bead toward you with the thumb for each repetition, and turn back at the guru bead.
Tulsi beads are traditional for Vishnu and Krishna, rudraksha for Shiva.
The beads keep count so your attention can stay with the mantra and the breath.

faq.q: What are the basic japa mala rules?
faq.a: Hold the mala in the right hand, often over the middle finger, and move beads toward you with the thumb. Begin at the bead next to the guru bead and say one mantra per bead. At the guru bead, turn the mala and go back rather than crossing it. Keep the mala clean, and many people store it in a cloth bag.

faq.q: Which finger to use for a mala?
faq.a: Most traditions drape the mala over the middle or ring finger of the right hand and move the beads with the thumb. The index finger is traditionally kept away from the beads, since it is associated with the ego in many teachings. Some traditions vary. If one hand is injured or tired, using the other hand is perfectly acceptable.

faq.q: Should I choose a rudraksha vs tulsi mala?
faq.a: Tradition links rudraksha beads with Shiva and tulsi beads with Vishnu and Krishna, so many people match the mala to the mantra. Sandalwood and crystal malas are also common. If you are unsure, choose the one that feels good in the hand and suits the mantra you already chant. Keeping one mala for one practice helps build the habit.

posts.title: Pranayama Before Pooja: Three Breaths That Settle
posts.description: Pranayama before puja in three simple breaths: why the tradition begins worship with the breath, how to do it seated, and what to skip if you feel unwell.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Most poojas begin with the breath, not the flowers; try three slow breaths before you light the lamp tomorrow and notice how different the next five minutes feel.

## Why does worship start with pranayama? — in sandhyavandanam and many home poojas, a short pranayama comes right after achamanam, sipping water, and before the sankalpam; the tradition treats a settled breath as the doorway

## Pranayama before puja: three breaths that settle — sit upright; one slow breath in through the nose and a longer breath out; one breath through alternate nostrils, nadi shodhana, using thumb and ring finger; one breath held gently before the exhale

## What if breathing exercises make you uncomfortable? — never strain or hold the breath forcefully; skip retention if you are pregnant, have high blood pressure or a heart condition, and ask your doctor; plain slow breathing is enough
Close: Try this for a week: three breaths, then the lamp; the practice is small on purpose
takeaways: Many traditional poojas begin with a short pranayama, a breath practice, to settle the body before the prayer begins.
Three slow breaths, with the exhale longer than the inhale, are enough for a home pooja.
Never strain; skip breath-holding if you have a health condition and check with your doctor.

faq.q: What is a simple pranayama for beginners before prayer?
faq.a: Sit upright and breathe in slowly through the nose for a count of four, then breathe out for a count of six. Repeat three times. If you like, add one round of alternate-nostril breathing using the right thumb and ring finger. Keep it gentle, with no strain. Then light the lamp or begin your prayer while the breath is still slow.

faq.q: How do I do nadi shodhana before puja?
faq.a: Close the right nostril with the thumb and breathe in through the left. Close the left with the ring finger, release the right, and breathe out. Breathe in through the right, switch, and breathe out through the left. That is one round. Two or three rounds before a pooja are plenty. Stop if you feel dizzy and breathe normally.

faq.q: Is it necessary to do pranayama before every pooja?
faq.a: No. It is part of formal rituals such as sandhyavandanam and is commonly included in longer home poojas, but a sincere prayer without it is still a prayer. Many people find that even a few slow breaths make the ritual feel less rushed. Think of it as helpful preparation, not a rule that invalidates worship if skipped.

posts.title: Mouna Vratam: A Day of Silence, Tried Honestly
posts.description: Mouna vratam, a vow of silence, tried honestly: what the tradition says, how to plan a half day or a full day of silence at home, and what you may notice.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Mouna vratam is a vow of silence, and the first thing you notice is not peace but how often you were about to speak; try four hours before you try a day.

## What is mouna vratam in the tradition? — mouna, silence, kept as a vow on chosen days such as Mondays, Ekadashi or Mouni Amavasya, the new moon of Magha; sages known for long silence, and the teaching that silence is itself a form of prayer
## How do you plan a day of silence at home? — tell the household in advance, pick a morning, keep phones and messages off too, keep simple tasks, allow gestures for safety and emergencies
## What do people notice in silence? — the urge to comment, to explain, to fill; the voice in the head gets louder, then quieter; listening changes; many find they speak more carefully afterwards
Close: Try this for a week: one hour of silence each evening, then a half day at the weekend; notice which words you actually missed
takeaways: Mouna vratam is a vow of silence kept for a set time, traditionally on days like Mondays, Ekadashi or Mouni Amavasya.
Start with a few hours, tell your household, and include phones and messages in the silence.
The first thing silence shows you is how often you were about to speak.

faq.q: What is a vow of silence in Hinduism?
faq.a: In Hindu practice, mouna vratam is a vow to refrain from speech for a chosen period, from an hour to a day or longer. It is kept on days such as Mondays, Ekadashi or Mouni Amavasya, and by some sages for years. Silence is seen as a way to conserve energy, calm the mind and turn attention inward toward prayer.

faq.q: What is Mouni Amavasya?
faq.a: Mouni Amavasya is the new-moon day in the lunar month of Magha, usually in January or February. Many devotees keep silence for part or all of the day, bathe in a sacred river if they can, and give charity. The name comes from mouna, silence. Check the panchangam each year for the exact day, as it follows the lunar calendar.

faq.q: What are the spiritual benefits of silence?
faq.a: People who keep silence regularly describe a quieter mind, sharper listening and more careful speech afterwards. The tradition says silence gathers energy that talking scatters, and prepares the mind for prayer or meditation. These are experiences rather than promises. A few hours of real silence, including screens, is enough to notice something for yourself.

posts.title: Why 108 Is Sacred: The Number Behind the Beads
posts.description: Why 108 is sacred in Hindu practice: the beads, the 27 stars and four padas, the names and the temples, and why the number works so well for the body.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: A mala has 108 beads, a stotram has 108 names, a pilgrimage may cover 108 temples; nobody fully agrees why 108 is sacred, and that is part of what makes it interesting to look at honestly.

## Why 108 is sacred: the traditional reasons — 27 nakshatras times four padas each; 12 rasis times nine grahas; the 108 Divya Desams of Vishnu; ashtottaram, the 108-name hymns; a traditional list of 108 Upanishads

## What about the astronomy claims? — the often-cited idea that the Sun's distance is about 108 times its diameter, and the Moon's roughly the same; approximately true, a lovely coincidence, not a proof
## Why does 108 work for the body? — a round of 108 takes long enough, around ten to fifteen minutes for a short mantra, for the breath to slow and the mind to wander and return several times
Close: Try this for a week: one round of 108 each morning; notice around which bead the mind first goes quiet
takeaways: 108 is sacred in Hindu practice partly because 27 nakshatras times four padas, and 12 rasis times nine grahas, both give 108.
Many hymns have 108 names, and Vishnu's 108 Divya Desams are a traditional pilgrimage.
A round of 108 repetitions takes long enough for the breath and mind to settle.

faq.q: What is the 108 beads meaning in a mala?
faq.a: A mala of 108 beads lets you count 108 repetitions of a mantra, a number sacred in Hindu, Buddhist and Jain practice. The extra larger bead, the guru or meru bead, marks the start and end of the round. Reasons given for 108 include 27 lunar stars times four quarters each, and 12 zodiac signs times nine planets.

faq.q: Why chant a mantra 108 times?
faq.a: Tradition treats 108 as a complete cycle, so a mantra repeated 108 times is considered one full offering. Practically, a round of 108 takes long enough for the breath to slow and the mind to settle, wander and return several times. If 108 is too many for now, 27 or 54, fractions of 108, are also traditional.

faq.q: What is the significance of 108 in Hinduism?
faq.a: 108 appears across Hindu practice: 108 names in ashtottaram hymns, 108 Divya Desams sacred to Vishnu, a traditional list of 108 Upanishads, and 108 beads on a mala. In Jyotish, 27 nakshatras with four padas each make 108, as do 12 rasis times nine grahas. It is a number of completeness rather than a mathematical secret.

posts.title: Trataka: Lamp Gazing as a Practice of Attention
posts.description: Trataka meditation, lamp gazing step by step: where the practice comes from, how to sit with a flame for a few minutes, and who should skip or adapt it.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Trataka meditation is simple enough to try tonight: a lamp at eye level, arm's length away, and your eyes resting on the flame until they water; then close them and watch what stays.
## What is trataka meditation? — one of the six cleansing practices, the shatkarmas, described in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika; steady gazing at a small point, most often a flame

## How do you do trataka at home? — a ghee lamp or candle in a dark, draught-free room; sit upright, gaze without straining, blink when needed, then close the eyes and hold the afterimage; start with one to three minutes

## Who should skip or adapt it? — people with eye conditions, recent eye surgery, migraines, epilepsy or seizure history should avoid flame gazing and ask a doctor; gaze at a dot instead; never push through discomfort
Close: Try this for a week, three minutes each evening before bed; notice whether it is easier to stay with one thing the next day
takeaways: Trataka is steady gazing at a small point, usually a lamp flame, described as a cleansing practice in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika.
Start with one to three minutes, gaze without strain, then close the eyes and rest on the afterimage.
Skip flame gazing if you have eye conditions, migraines or a seizure history, and ask your doctor.

faq.q: How to do trataka for beginners?
faq.a: Place a ghee lamp or candle at eye level about an arm's length away in a dim, still room. Sit upright and rest your gaze on the flame without straining. Blink if you need to. After one to three minutes, close your eyes and watch the afterimage until it fades. Repeat once more. Increase the time slowly over weeks.

faq.q: Is candle gazing meditation safe?
faq.a: For most people a few minutes is safe, but avoid it if you have an eye condition, recent eye surgery, migraines, epilepsy or a history of seizures, and ask your doctor if unsure. Never force the eyes open until they hurt. A black dot on a wall is a gentler alternative. Keep the flame away from curtains and never leave it unattended.

faq.q: Does trataka help with concentration?
faq.a: Many people who practise trataka describe steadier attention and an easier time settling into tasks, which is how the tradition describes it too. These are reported experiences rather than promises. Try three minutes each evening for a week and notice whether it becomes easier to stay with one thing, a conversation, a page or a task, the next day.

posts.title: Likhita Japa: Writing a Mantra in a Notebook

## What is likhita japa? — likhita, written; japa, repetition; the tradition of writing a name or mantra many times, such as Sri Rama Jayam or Om Namah Shivaya; the Rama Koti practice of aiming for a crore of names, often offered at temples
## How do you begin likhita japa? — one notebook kept only for this, one pen, the same mantra, a few lines a day; neatness matters more than speed; say the words silently as you write
## Why does writing slow the mind down? — the hand is slower than thought, so the mind has to wait for it; you can see where your attention wandered on the page
Close: One small thing to carry into this week: write one line of your mantra before you open your laptop each morning
takeaways: Likhita japa is writing a mantra or divine name by hand, again and again, such as Sri Rama Jayam.
Keep one notebook and pen for it, write a few lines daily, and say the words silently as you write.
Because the hand is slower than thought, writing a mantra gives a busy mind something steady to follow.

faq.q: What is Sri Rama Jayam writing?
faq.a: Sri Rama Jayam writing is a popular form of likhita japa in South India, where devotees write the phrase, meaning victory to Rama, many times in a notebook. Children are often taught to write it at the top of exam papers or before starting work. Some write it daily as a practice of devotion and focus, filling notebook after notebook.

faq.q: What are the rules for writing a mantra in a notebook?
faq.a: Keep a clean notebook used only for the mantra, and a pen kept for the purpose. Write neatly, one mantra per line or in a set pattern, saying the words silently. Sit in a clean place if you can, but a train seat works too. Do not rush. Many keep filled notebooks respectfully or offer them at a temple.

faq.q: What is Rama Koti writing?
faq.a: Rama Koti is a devotional vow to write the name of Rama a koti, ten million times, often over many years and with family members joining in. Completed notebooks are traditionally offered at temples associated with Rama. Many people set smaller personal targets, such as one notebook or one hundred thousand names, which is also a meaningful practice.

posts.title: Surya Namaskar Meaning: A Greeting, Not a Workout

posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: Surya namaskar means salutation to the Sun, and its meaning changes when you stop counting rounds and start saying a name with each one; try six slow rounds facing east tomorrow.
## Surya namaskar meaning: a greeting, not a workout — namaskar as bowing; twelve positions flowing with the breath; traditionally done at sunrise, facing east, before food

## What are the twelve names of Surya? — Mitra, Ravi, Surya, Bhanu, Khaga, Pusha, Hiranyagarbha, Marichi, Aditya, Savitri, Arka, Bhaskara, each said with one position, each a quality of the Sun: friend, radiant, nourisher
## How do you practise it gently? — slow over fast, breath leading movement, knees down when needed; skip or adapt with back, knee or blood pressure concerns, during pregnancy, and ask a doctor
Close: Try this for a week: six rounds at dawn, one name per position; notice whether your mornings start differently
takeaways: Surya namaskar means salutation to the Sun, a sequence of twelve positions offered as a greeting at sunrise.
Traditionally each position is paired with one of twelve names of Surya, such as Mitra, Ravi and Bhaskara.
Practise slowly with the breath, and adapt or skip it if you have back, knee or blood pressure concerns.

faq.q: What are the surya namaskar mantras?
faq.a: Each of the twelve positions is traditionally paired with a name of the Sun, preceded by Om and followed by namaha: Mitra, Ravi, Surya, Bhanu, Khaga, Pusha, Hiranyagarbha, Marichi, Aditya, Savitri, Arka and Bhaskara. For example, Om Mitraya Namaha, salutation to the friend of all. Saying them aloud or silently turns the sequence into a prayer.

faq.q: What is the spiritual meaning of the sun salutation?
faq.a: In Hindu tradition, the Sun is the visible form of the divine that sustains all life, and the Aditya Hrudayam praises it as every god in one. Surya namaskar is a bow to that source at the start of the day. Moving with the breath and a name in each position makes it a moving meditation rather than exercise.

faq.q: Is surya namaskar safe for everyone?
faq.a: It suits many people when practised slowly, but it involves forward bends, weight on the arms and back bends. If you have back or knee problems, high blood pressure, are pregnant or recovering from surgery, ask your doctor and a qualified teacher first. Adapting positions, such as keeping knees down, is fine. The intention of greeting the Sun matters most.

posts.title: Why We Sit on the Floor to Pray (and Chairs Are Fine)

outline: Hook: Sitting on the floor to pray lowers the body, steadies the spine and brings you level with the lamp; and if your knees say no, a chair does the job too.

## Why sit on the floor for puja? — asana means seat as well as posture; the tradition of sitting on a mat of darbha grass, wool or cloth rather than bare ground; a low seat that keeps the body still and the gaze level with the shrine
## What does the body notice on the floor? — crossed legs in sukhasana ground the hips; a stable base lets the breath drop lower; fewer distractions when getting up takes effort
## Can I do puja sitting on a chair? — yes: knees, hips, pregnancy, age and injury are reasons enough; sit upright, feet flat, a small shrine raised to eye level; the attention is what matters
Close: Try this for a week: sit on a folded blanket for five minutes of prayer, then try a chair on another day; notice which lets you be most still
takeaways: Tradition asks you to sit on a mat on the floor for puja because a low, stable seat keeps the body still and the gaze level with the shrine.
Sitting in a chair is perfectly fine if your knees, hips or health need it.
Upright spine and steady attention matter more than where you sit.

faq.q: Can I do puja sitting on a chair?
faq.a: Yes. Many elders, people with knee or hip trouble, pregnant women and anyone recovering from injury do their prayers in a chair. Sit upright with feet flat, and raise the shrine or lamp to a comfortable eye level if you can. Traditions value attention and sincerity over posture. A settled, comfortable body usually prays better than a strained one.

faq.q: Why is an asana mat used for puja?
faq.a: Tradition asks that you not sit directly on bare ground for worship. A mat of darbha grass, wool, cotton or silk, called an asana, marks a clean, dedicated seat. Many keep one mat only for prayer, which becomes a cue for the body and mind. A folded blanket or a small cushion works well in modern homes.

faq.q: Is sukhasana good for prayer?
faq.a: Sukhasana, the easy cross-legged pose, is the most common seat for home prayer because it is stable and needs no special flexibility. Sitting on a folded blanket so the hips are higher than the knees makes it more comfortable for longer periods. If your legs go numb, change position or use a low stool. Comfort supports attention.

posts.title: Sattvic Diet Explained: Food That Leaves You Clear

posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: A sattvic diet is not a menu; it is a question you ask after eating: do I feel clear, restless or heavy? Try asking it for a week and you will understand the idea better than any list.

## What is a sattvic diet? — sattva, the quality of clarity and balance, one of the three gunas with rajas (activity, restlessness) and tamas (inertia, heaviness); food read through the same lens; fresh, lightly cooked, moderate

## What does the Bhagavad Gita say about food? — the seventeenth chapter describes foods dear to the sattvic as those that are juicy, wholesome and pleasing, the rajasic as too bitter, sour, salty, hot or pungent, and the tamasic as stale or spoiled; the Gita describes, it does not command

## A sattvic food list, and its limits — fresh vegetables and fruit, whole grains, lentils, milk, ghee, nuts, mild spices; onion, garlic, meat, alcohol and leftovers commonly left out in temple traditions; views differ, and this is tradition, not medical advice
Close: For one week, eat dinner a little earlier, a little fresher and a little smaller, and write down, in your head, how the mornings feel.
takeaways: A sattvic diet favours fresh, simple, moderately spiced food that tradition says leaves the mind clear rather than restless or heavy.
The Bhagavad Gita's seventeenth chapter describes sattvic, rajasic and tamasic foods; it is a description of tendencies, not a rulebook.

faq.q: What is on a sattvic food list?
faq.a: A typical sattvic food list includes fresh fruits and vegetables, whole grains such as rice and wheat, lentils and mung beans, milk, curd, ghee, nuts, seeds, honey and mild spices like cumin, turmeric and ginger. Temple and yogic traditions usually leave out onion, garlic, meat, alcohol, and stale or reheated food.

faq.q: What is the difference between sattvic rajasic tamasic food?
faq.a: In Hindu tradition, sattvic food is fresh, light and nourishing and is said to support calm and clarity. Rajasic food is very spicy, salty, sour or stimulating and is linked with restlessness. Tamasic food is stale, overcooked or intoxicating and is associated with heaviness. These are traditional categories, not medical classifications.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about food?
faq.a: In its seventeenth chapter, the Bhagavad Gita describes three kinds of food matching the three gunas. Food dear to the sattvic is juicy, wholesome and pleasing; rajasic food is excessively bitter, sour, salty or hot; tamasic food is stale, tasteless or spoiled. The Gita presents this as observation of human tendency, not a list of commandments.

faq.q: Can I follow a sattvic diet while living in the US?
faq.a: Yes. A sattvic approach is less about specific Indian ingredients and more about freshness, simplicity and moderation. Cook at home when you can, choose seasonal produce, eat earlier in the evening and avoid heavily processed food. Anyone with a medical condition should talk to a doctor before making major dietary changes.

posts.title: Why No Onion or Garlic in Hindu Pooja Food?
posts.description: Why no onion or garlic in Hindu pooja food? The guna idea, the Rahu and Ketu folk story, temple kitchens, and why many homes skip them only on pooja days.
posts.author: archana
outline: Hook: The short answer: many Hindu traditions class onion and garlic as rajasic or tamasic, foods said to stir or dull the mind, so they are left out of offerings. The longer answer is more interesting, and you can test part of it in your own kitchen.

## Why no onion or garlic in Hindu pooja food? — the three gunas applied to food; onion and garlic seen as strongly stimulating, so temple kitchens, Vaishnava homes and many families cooking naivedyam leave them out; customs vary, and many eat them daily and skip them only on pooja and fasting days

## Is there a story behind it? — a popular folk tale ties them to the churning of the ocean: when Rahu's head was cut off after he drank the nectar, drops fell to earth and became onion and garlic, potent but not pure; a story, not scripture, told to explain a practice

## What does cooking without onion and garlic do to your attention? — asafoetida, ginger, curry leaves and tempering carry flavour; many people find the food feels lighter and the kitchen smells different; Jain practice avoids root vegetables for a separate reason, non-harm to soil life
Close: Try one week of pooja-style cooking at dinner, no onion or garlic, and notice not what you miss but what you taste.
takeaways: Onion and garlic are left out of Hindu pooja food because many traditions class them as rajasic or tamasic, foods said to agitate or dull the mind.
The custom varies: temple kitchens and some families avoid them always, while many homes skip them only on pooja and fasting days.

faq.q: Is onion tamasic in Hinduism?
faq.a: Many Hindu and yogic traditions describe onion and garlic as rajasic, stimulating, or tamasic, dulling, depending on the school. That is why they are left out of temple food, naivedyam and fasting meals. It is a traditional classification rather than a health judgement, and practice varies widely, from strict avoidance to everyday use outside pooja days.

faq.q: What is the onion garlic Rahu Ketu story?
faq.a: A popular folk story connects onion and garlic to the churning of the ocean. The asura Rahu disguised himself to drink the nectar of immortality, and Vishnu cut off his head. Drops of nectar mixed with his blood fell to earth and grew into onion and garlic. It is a folk explanation, not found in major scriptures.

faq.q: How do I start cooking without onion and garlic?
faq.a: When cooking without onion and garlic, build flavour with a tempering of mustard, cumin and curry leaves, a pinch of asafoetida, fresh ginger, tomatoes, coconut and tamarind. South Indian temple recipes such as sambar, rasam, kootu, pongal and puliyodarai are naturally onion-free. Start with one or two dishes you already know and simply leave them out.

faq.q: Why do Jains not eat onion and garlic?
faq.a: Jains avoid onion, garlic and most root vegetables mainly because of ahimsa, non-harm. Pulling up a root kills the whole plant and disturbs many tiny organisms in the soil. This reason differs from the Hindu guna classification, although the result in the kitchen is similar. Jain practice varies in strictness among families.

posts.title: Eating on a Banana Leaf: Tradition and Attention

outline: Hook: A banana leaf changes how you eat before the first bite. It is wide, green, faintly fragrant when warm food touches it, and it asks you to eat with your hand and pay attention. Try it once at home.

## Eating on a banana leaf: which way, which place — the tapering end to the left of the diner in Tamil and Kerala custom, salt, pickle and small sides along the top, rice in the lower middle, sweet at the lower left; payasam on the leaf or in a cup

## Why a leaf and not a plate? — the tradition of leaves as clean, single-use and returned to earth; temples and weddings serving on leaves; many people find the aroma and the texture slow them down; the leaf as a shared custom across South India

## Where do you get banana leaves in the US, and how do you fold one? — frozen leaves at Asian, Latin and Indian grocery stores; thawing, wiping and warming over a flame to soften; folding the top half toward you after eating as a sign of satisfaction (at funerals it is folded away); customs vary
Close: For one dinner this week, cut a leaf, lay the meal out in order, eat with your hand, and fold it when you are done.
takeaways: On a traditional banana leaf, the narrow end points to the diner's left, side dishes run along the top, and rice sits in the lower centre.
After eating, folding the top half toward you signals the meal was good; frozen banana leaves are easy to find at Asian and Latin grocery stores.

faq.q: What is the banana leaf serving order in a South Indian meal?
faq.a: The banana leaf serving order usually begins with salt, pickle and small side dishes along the top edge, followed by vegetables, then rice in the lower centre with dal and ghee. Sambar, rasam and curd come in turns, with sweets and payasam placed on the lower left. Kerala sadyas and Tamil meals differ slightly.

faq.q: How do I fold a banana leaf after eating?
faq.a: To fold a banana leaf after eating, fold the top half down toward yourself over the leftovers. In Tamil and Kerala custom, this signals that you enjoyed the meal. Folding it away from you is traditionally reserved for funerals or sad occasions. Customs differ between families, so follow your host's lead if you are unsure.

faq.q: Where can I buy banana leaves in the USA?
faq.a: You can buy banana leaves in the USA at most Asian, Latin American and Indian grocery stores, usually frozen and sometimes fresh. Thaw them, rinse, wipe dry, and pass them briefly over a gas flame or warm skillet to make them soft and fragrant. Cut them into meal-size pieces with scissors.

faq.q: Which side of the banana leaf faces the diner?
faq.a: In South Indian custom, the narrow, tapering end of the leaf points to the diner's left, and the wider end to the right, so the right hand has room for rice. The glossy upper side faces up. Some regions have different habits, and hosts usually lay the leaf out before guests sit down.

faq.q: Why do Indians eat with hands?

Tradition sees touch as part of tasting, and eating with the hand as a more personal, attentive way to receive food. Many cultures across Asia and Africa share the custom.

faq.q: How do I eat rice with my hand without making a mess?
faq.a: Use only your right hand. Mix a small amount of rice with the gravy using your fingertips, not the palm. Press it into a loose ball, lift it on your first three fingers, and push it into your mouth with your thumb. Start with thicker dishes like dal rice or curd rice before trying rasam.

faq.q: Is eating with your hands a kind of mindful eating?
faq.a: It can be. Mindful eating with hands asks you to notice temperature, texture and amount before the food reaches your mouth, which naturally slows the meal. Many people find they chew more and notice fullness sooner. It is a practice of attention, and it works best without a phone or screen at the table.

faq.q: Is it hygienic to eat with your hands?
faq.a: Eating with your hands is hygienic when you wash them well with soap before and after the meal and keep nails short. Tradition also uses only the right hand for eating. Many families keep a jug of water near the table. If you are unwell or sharing food, use a spoon.
